title: How to keep a sinus symptom diary.
description: Track congestion, pressure, smell, sleep, and daily impact with a simple sinus symptom diary you can keep returning to.
answer: A useful sinus symptom diary records the date, how your symptoms feel, their impact on your day, and any changes to routines you already follow. Keep entries brief and use the same scale. Bring the history to a clinician; a diary can support a conversation but cannot identify the cause of your symptoms.

sections.title: Why keep a sinus symptom diary?
paragraphs: When you live with recurring congestion, reduced smell, or facial pressure, individual days can blur together. At an appointment, “it has been a difficult few weeks” may be true, but it can be hard to explain what changed and when.

A diary gives you a dated personal record. It may help you remember when symptoms started, whether they returned to your usual, and which parts of daily life felt different. It does not prove that weather, a routine, or a particular exposure caused a change.

sections.title: What should you write down?
paragraphs: Start with a small set of details you can record consistently. You can always add more when it is helpful.
items: Date and overall burden: choose a simple scale, such as none, mild, moderate, severe, or very severe.
Symptoms you notice: nasal blockage, drainage, reduced smell, facial pressure, or headache. Record headache separately rather than assuming its cause.
Daily impact: a short note about sleep, concentration, work, or an activity you missed.
Your existing routines: record what you actually did, and when a routine changed. Follow your clinician’s instructions rather than changing treatment based on the diary.
Context, if useful: a cold-like illness, travel, or outdoor conditions. Mark uncertain details as uncertain.

sections.title: Make room for “my usual.”
paragraphs: Your usual is not necessarily the same as having no symptoms. If you live with persistent congestion, a day that feels typical can still include symptoms.

Keep “compared with my usual” separate from an overall rating. For example, you might write “usual nasal blockage, moderate overall symptoms.” That helps preserve both the day-to-day change and the burden you are living with.
sections.quote: The goal is a clearer record of your experience, not a perfect score for how well you tracked it.

sections.title: A small routine is easier to return to.
paragraphs: Try recording your overall experience at a similar time, using the same wording and scale. An optional morning note can capture how you woke up; an evening note can describe the day as a whole.

Missed a day? Leave it blank or label a later entry as recalled. A missing entry does not mean you felt well. If daily tracking feels like too much, log a flare when it starts and note when you return to your usual.

sections.title: Take the story to your next visit.
paragraphs: Before your appointment, look for a few concrete things you want to discuss: a symptom that stayed different, a change in smell, disruption to sleep, or uncertainty about a routine.

A concise summary and a few questions may be easier to review than a long diary. Your clinician can decide what information is relevant and whether examination or other assessment is needed. Persistent or worsening symptoms deserve professional advice; tracking should never delay getting care.

sections.title: How to log a sinus flare-up from start to finish
paragraphs: When symptoms feel worse than your usual, note when you first noticed the change and what felt different. Add short updates on the days you check in. Leave the episode open until you observe a return to your usual, or write that you’re unsure when it settled.

sections.title: Give the episode a start and an end
paragraphs: Start with the earliest time you can reasonably place. “Tuesday morning” works if you can’t remember the hour. If you already felt worse when you woke up, “noticed on waking” is more precise than assuming it began overnight. Put the most noticeable change first. Add another symptom or one detail about sleep or daily impact if it helps you recognise the episode later.

An episode can still be open when you review your diary. Write “still worse at Friday’s check-in” rather than picking an end date. If you miss a check-in, keep the gap visible. An approximate end range is fine when all you know is the last worse day and the first day back to usual.

sections.title: A worked flare-up timeline
paragraphs: In a summary, write “worse on Tuesday and Thursday, Wednesday unknown, back to my usual by Friday morning”. That preserves the timeline without counting Wednesday as a confirmed symptomatic day. On days when symptoms fluctuate, a line such as “felt better at lunch, worse again by evening” can stay inside the same episode entry.

If you keep notes on your phone, AirBloom is being built to put flare notes next to ordinary check-ins, including the days you leave blank. That makes the return to your own baseline easier to see when you look back.

sections.title: Compare episodes using the same labels
paragraphs: When looking back, pick the dates, the main change and the impact that mattered most. If you’re still unsure whether symptoms returned to usual between two difficult stretches, keep that uncertainty in the summary you bring to your doctor. The NHS sinusitis guide explains when to seek advice for symptoms that keep returning or become worse.

sections.title: How to rate sinus symptom severity consistently
paragraphs: A simple way to rate sinus symptoms in a diary is to record how much one symptom got in the way at the time you checked. Use the same labels each time and leave missed checks marked as unknown. The scale below is for comparing your own entries.

sections.title: A personal scale you can reuse
paragraphs: Choose a symptom before giving it a rating. Write “blockage 2, pressure 0” if blockage interrupted something and you checked for pressure and felt none. Leave pressure unknown if you skipped that question. If the blockage is usually a 1 for you, “my usual” can sit next to that number as a separate note.

sections.title: Compare entries made at similar times
paragraphs: Use the same check-in time when that’s practical. If you write “blockage 1” in the morning and “blockage 3” that evening, keep both times. At the end of the week, try a sentence such as “blockage interrupted something on two of my five recorded mornings.” Keep the two unrecorded mornings visible.

Clinics may use questionnaires with their own questions and scoring rules. Bring your diary as a record of what you experienced, and fill out any clinic questionnaire using the instructions they give you.

sections.title: What to write in a sinus diary on good days
paragraphs: On a good day, record whether you felt clear, about your usual or better than usual. If you missed the check, mark it as unrecorded. A blank entry and a day you actually checked tell two different stories.

sections.title: Keep the good day in the same diary
paragraphs: Use the same time and fields you use on rough days. A quick note such as “clear at breakfast” is enough. If you normally wake up a little blocked and feel that way today, record “my usual” rather than calling it symptom-free. If you only checked at breakfast, keep that time beside the note.

sections.title: Read the same week two ways
paragraphs: Imagine you recorded five of seven mornings. Two were worse than usual, one was your usual and two were clear. “Two worse mornings out of seven” can sound as though you checked every morning. A more precise summary is “two worse, one usual and two clear out of five mornings recorded. Two mornings unknown.”

If you compare two weeks, keep each denominator. “Two of five recorded mornings” and “two of two recorded mornings” are different amounts of information. You can give both counts without trying to estimate the missing days.

A dated clear check-in can help you describe when a flare ended. If the last worse day was Monday and the next clear check was Thursday, write “clear by Thursday”. Leave the days between open if you did not check.

title: How to prepare for an ENT appointment.
description: A thoughtful checklist to bring your symptoms, routines, and questions into the same conversation.
answer: To prepare for an ENT appointment about sinus symptoms, bring a short symptom timeline, a current medication and routine list, relevant previous records, and your most important questions. Include how symptoms affect sleep, smell, and daily life. Follow the clinic’s preparation instructions and let the clinician guide diagnosis and treatment.

sections.title: Start with the story you want to tell.
paragraphs: An appointment can feel short when you have months of experiences to explain. You do not need to arrive with a diagnosis or a perfectly organized folder. A few dated notes can help you describe what has been happening.
Write one or two sentences in your own words: “My nose feels blocked most days, and my sense of smell changed about two months ago.” Include what you most want help understanding.

sections.title: 1. Bring a simple symptom timeline.
paragraphs: Note when symptoms began, whether they are persistent or come in bouts, and whether there are clear intervals when you return to your usual. Use approximate dates when you do not remember exactly.
items: Which symptoms you notice, and whether they affect one side or both.
Changes in smell, nasal blockage, drainage, facial pressure, and headache, recorded separately.
Effects on sleep, energy, concentration, and activities.
Any major changes, procedures, or previous clinician assessments you want to discuss.

sections.title: 2. List what you already use.
paragraphs: Bring the names of prescription medicines, over-the-counter products, supplements, rinses, or sprays you currently use. Include the schedule as you actually follow it and, where possible, when it started or changed.

Photographs of packaging can help you remember product names. Avoid guessing an ingredient or dose. Your care team can help clarify uncertain information. Do not stop or change a treatment for the appointment unless the clinic or your clinician tells you to.

sections.title: 3. Choose the questions that matter most.
paragraphs: A short question list can help you return to your priorities during the conversation. Here are a few starting points to adapt:
items: What might explain these symptoms, and what would help distinguish the possibilities?
Does the change in my sense of smell need further assessment?
Which details in my symptom history are most useful to track?
How should I follow the plan we agree on, and when should we review it?
What changes should prompt me to contact the clinic or seek urgent help?
sections.quote: You do not have to explain everything perfectly. Your lived experience is a useful place to start.

sections.title: 4. Check the practical details.
paragraphs: Ask the clinic which previous records are useful and how to send them securely. Depending on your history, they may want reports, previous imaging, allergy testing, or information from another clinician. Do not arrange tests yourself just to complete a checklist.
Confirm appointment time, referral requirements, accessibility needs, and any clinic-specific preparation. Consider bringing someone you trust if that would help you remember the conversation.

sections.title: Leave with a plan in your own words.
paragraphs: Before the visit ends, ask about anything that is unclear. You can repeat the agreed next steps back in your own words and ask when a follow-up is needed.
AirBloom is being designed to help turn your own records into an editable visit summary. You will choose what to include and share. It is a way to prepare your story, not a clinical assessment.

sections.title: Questions about the plan you discuss at an ENT visit
paragraphs: Ask what the proposed plan is intended to address, how to follow it, what observations are useful and when it should be reviewed. Bring what you have actually tried and any uncertainty about effects. Let the clinician guide individual treatment choices.

sections.title: Organize questions around your own record
paragraphs: A list of every possible treatment can crowd out the question you most need answered. Start with the current problem and what you want the consultation to clarify. The NHS recommends preparing questions and asking for explanations when information is unclear.

Bring the exact names of products you use and describe how you have actually used them. If you do not know an ingredient or cannot remember a start date, mark it uncertain. Do not infer that a change after a routine proves an effect.

sections.title: Leave with the next step in your own words
paragraphs: Repeat the agreed plan back in a way you understand. Ask which changes should prompt a contact and use the clinic’s own contact route. A question card is not a recommendation to start, stop or compare medicines independently.

If a question remains unresolved, write it down rather than filling the gap from memory after the appointment. The medication-list checklist holds exact product details; the routine log holds longitudinal observations. Keep both separate from a decision about which treatment is right for you.

sections.title: A medication and product list for an ENT appointment
paragraphs: Bring exact product names, how you actually use them and approximate start or change dates. Include prescribed and over-the-counter products relevant to the conversation. Mark uncertain details and follow the clinic’s instructions about preparation.

sections.title: Use the packaging to preserve the name
paragraphs: Different products can have similar names or packaging. Copy the exact name rather than guessing what a spray contains. A photograph of packaging may help if your clinic accepts it through its normal process. Keep personal details off any publicly shared example or downloadable blank form.

The list is a prompt for the consultation, not a medication review. Follow existing instructions and do not stop or change a product to make the list simpler. Ask the clinic what to bring if you are unsure about preparation.

sections.title: Keep the record useful and proportionate
paragraphs: Add a note about products prescribed elsewhere or bought without a prescription when relevant to the conversation. Let the care team decide which details matter. A complete-looking invented date is less useful than “started sometime in October.”

The product list answers “what do I use?” The routine log answers “what did I actually use at a recorded time?” The doctor summary answers “what changed and what do I want to discuss?” Keeping those tasks separate prevents a one-page appointment sheet from becoming a lengthy daily diary.

title: Why do my sinus symptoms change day to day?
description: A practical way to track congestion, sleep, outdoor conditions, and routine changes without jumping to conclusions about your triggers.
answer: A blocked nose or facial pressure can vary for different reasons, and similar symptoms do not always have the same cause. A consistent diary can help you compare your symptoms with sleep, routines, illnesses, and outdoor conditions. Repeated patterns are useful questions to explore; they are not proof of a trigger or a reliable forecast of how you will feel tomorrow.

sections.title: Start with the symptoms, not a guess about the cause.
paragraphs: “My sinuses are bad today” can mean different things: a blocked nose, pressure, a change in smell, poor sleep, or several things at once. Give each symptom its own short entry so a single score does not hide the details.

The NHS lists blocked or runny nose, facial tenderness, and reduced smell among sinusitis symptoms. Allergic rhinitis can also involve a blocked or runny nose. A diary cannot tell you which condition you have.

sections.title: How can I spot useful patterns in my symptom history?
paragraphs: Pick a small set of details and use the same labels each time. For example, rate congestion on waking, then add a separate note about sleep and anything that changed in your normal routine.
When you look back, compare several recorded days rather than one memorable flare. Keep missing days visible: no entry is not the same as no symptoms.
items: Record the symptom and time before adding context.
Separate what happened from what you think caused it.
Compare days with a similar level of detail.
Keep uncertainty in the note: “possibly more blocked after the walk.”

sections.title: What can pollen and air-quality information tell me?
paragraphs: For people with allergic rhinitis, pollen is one possible allergen; the NHS also lists dust mites, animal dander, and mould. That does not mean all congestion is caused by allergy.

An air-quality index reports outdoor pollution conditions. It is not a measurement of your nose, a pollen count, or a personalized sinusitis score. Save the location and date alongside any environmental value, and treat it as context for your own record.

sections.title: Can an app predict how my sinusitis will feel today?
paragraphs: A morning overview can bring your recent entries, current check-in, and local conditions into one place. That is useful context for planning your day, but it is different from a clinically validated personal prediction.

AirBloom’s daily outlook is being designed around this distinction: your own history first, with uncertainty made clear. It will not guarantee a symptom-free day or tell you to change medication because of a forecast.

sections.title: Turn an observation into one useful next step.
paragraphs: Instead of trying to solve every flare at once, write down one question you want to understand. “Does this happen on the days I sleep poorly?” is easier to explore than “What causes everything?”

Seek professional advice for symptoms that persist, keep returning, or get worse. If you feel very unwell or pain relief does not help, follow local urgent-care advice. Do not wait for a diary pattern before getting help.

title: A simpler way to remember your sinus medication routine.
description: Keep your existing treatment instructions, reminders, and taken-or-missed notes together without letting an app decide your dose.
answer: A medication reminder should help you follow the instructions you already have from a clinician, pharmacist, or medicine leaflet. Record the exact product and agreed schedule, use a reminder you can recognize, and distinguish “reminded” from “taken.” An app should not choose a medicine, alter a dose, or invent advice for a missed dose.

sections.title: Start with one reliable list.
paragraphs: A routine is harder to follow when instructions are spread across packaging, notes, and memory. Make one list of what you currently use, with the product name and the schedule you were given.
If you are unsure which product you have or how to use it, check the leaflet or ask a pharmacist. Similar-looking nasal sprays can contain different types of medicine.
items: Exact product name, with a packaging photo if useful.
Your existing instructions and who provided them.
A start date, review date, or stop date when one was given.
A note of questions to clarify with your pharmacist or clinician.

sections.title: A reminder is not a prescription.
paragraphs: Choose a reminder label that tells you which existing routine it refers to. Use the timing specified in your treatment instructions; do not change that timing just to fit a notification.
AirBloom’s reminder features are being designed to keep your agreed routine visible. The app will not independently recommend a dose or decide that a symptom score means you need another medicine.

sections.title: Keep “taken,” “missed,” and “not sure” separate.
paragraphs: A notification arriving does not mean you used the medicine. Log what actually happened, and leave room for uncertainty rather than filling a gap with a guess.
If you miss a dose, consult the leaflet for that particular medicine or ask a pharmacist. Do not assume the same missed-dose instruction applies to every spray, tablet, or treatment.

sections.title: Check limits for the product you actually use.
paragraphs: The NHS warns that prolonged use of decongestant nasal sprays and drops can worsen a blocked nose. Check the limit in your exact product leaflet or ask a pharmacist. This warning is specific to decongestants; it is not a general schedule for all nasal products.
Check the current leaflet and speak with a pharmacist if you are uncertain about a product or if symptoms worsen. A reminder should preserve a review or stop instruction, not silently repeat forever.

sections.title: Keep your routine beside your symptom history.
paragraphs: A dated record can make it easier to remember when a routine changed and what you noticed afterwards. It can also help you explain what you actually followed, rather than what was intended.
A change in symptoms after a routine change does not prove the routine caused it. Use the record to ask clearer questions, and keep treatment decisions with your care team.

sections.title: Your seven-day sinus diary
paragraphs: Copy this table into a spreadsheet or use the full-size printable worksheet. Start on any date. Use a second sheet if you want to keep going into the following week.

A completed row might read: “7 Sep, worse than usual, left side more blocked, pressure around left cheek after lunch, smell unchanged, woke once overnight.” Use words you’d naturally say to someone else. In the blockage column, “left more than right” is often easier to record than trying to assign each side a number.

tables.caption: Your seven-day sinus diary

sections.title: Choose a baseline you can recognise
paragraphs: Clear means you noticed no symptoms you want to track at the check-in. My usual means the symptoms were about what you normally experience. If you’re often a little blocked, a typical blocked day belongs here. Better than usual and worse than usual describe a change from your own baseline. If you didn’t check, write not recorded.

Keep those labels consistent so you can compare entries later. If you feel clear at breakfast and blocked in the evening, keep the original check-in and add the evening change with an approximate time. That tells a different story from being blocked all day.

sections.title: Add detail only where it earns its place
paragraphs: For pressure, write where you felt it and whether it came and went. For smell, choose normal for you, reduced, changed or unsure. If the day was affected, put down one example. “Stopped twice on a walk to blow my nose” is easier to remember and describe later than “bad day”. The NHS sinusitis guide explains why symptoms such as blockage, facial discomfort and changes in smell are worth mentioning in a clinical conversation.

Use the context space for details you can place in time, such as a cold starting that week or a later-than-usual bedtime. If you routinely use a spray or rinse, give it a separate log when you need more space. Record what you observed alongside the symptom, leaving the reason open.

If you prefer keeping notes on a phone, AirBloom is being built around short daily check-ins and a timeline of the symptoms, sleep and routines you choose to record. The printable version gives you the same starting habit with a pen and one row a day.

sections.title: Make the sheet work for you
paragraphs: Check in around the same time when you can. Use the optional nights worksheet if symptoms and broken sleep tend to occur together. For a day you missed, resist the urge to complete it from a rough impression at the end of the week. Add a later note only if you remember a specific detail, and mark it as recalled.

Before you copy the diary for another week, count the days you actually logged and circle one or two entries that show a change. If you’re preparing for a visit, turn those entries into a one-page summary. The daily record stays available if your clinician asks about a specific date.

sections.title: What a partly completed week can show
paragraphs: Say you fill in four of seven rows. On Monday you marked “my usual”. On Tuesday and Thursday you marked “worse” and noted that your nose was more blocked on the left. On Sunday you marked “clear”. A fair summary would be “left side more blocked on two of four check-ins”. You have two dated examples to talk about and three days you can leave open.

If you’re tracking a flare, give the episode its own short note and refer back to the daily entries. Start with the first time you noticed the change. If you only know you felt better by Sunday, write “better by Sunday”. The diary can show the order in which you noticed things, even when a few dates are missing. The guide to keeping a sinus symptom diary has a worked flare timeline.

sections.title: How long should I track?
paragraphs: Seven days is a convenient page size. If that week misses the problem you want to describe, keep a second sheet if it helps. Use the NHS guidance on when to seek advice if symptoms persist or get worse while you’re tracking.

sections.title: A sleep diary for recurring sinus symptoms
paragraphs: Add a nights worksheet to your sinus diary if you want to compare how your nose feels before bed, what you remember about the night and how you feel the next morning. Use one row per night and date it by the evening it began. A wearable’s sleep estimate can sit beside your own notes in a separate field.

sections.title: The optional nights worksheet
paragraphs: On Wednesday, the wearable has an estimate but the writer made no symptom entries. On Thursday, the night itself is unknown, although there is a waking check-in. “No awakenings recalled” means that you don’t remember waking. Use “not recorded” if you skipped the question.

tables.caption: The optional nights worksheet

sections.title: Write down what you can place in time
paragraphs: At bedtime, note the time and how blocked you feel. In the morning, note whether you remember waking, how your nose feels and anything that mattered overnight. “Woke with a dry mouth and drank water” gives more detail than “slept badly”. If you add a device estimate, put it in its own column so you can tell it apart from what you remember.

sections.title: Look for examples you can describe
paragraphs: Pick a night with a bedtime and waking note. Then find one that looks different. If you want to discuss the pattern, say what happened on each occasion and how many nights you recorded. For a fuller record of sleep times and daytime tiredness, use the NHLBI sleep diary. If morning blockage is your main concern, try the on-waking and after-getting-up check-in for more detail.

sections.title: Use the editable sinus diary spreadsheet
paragraphs: Use one row for each planned check, keep labels consistent and distinguish unknown checks from blank rows. The editable spreadsheet provides separate blank and fictional-example tabs. It can organize observations but cannot interpret a symptom pattern clinically.

sections.title: Start with the blank tab
paragraphs: Download the workbook and use the Diary tab for your own record. The Example tab contains fictional entries only. Save your own copy before editing and keep it in a location appropriate for personal health notes. Review sharing permissions if you use a cloud spreadsheet service.

The field order is date, status, nasal blockage, facial pressure, sense of smell, sleep observation and routine or daily impact. Add short observations in your own words. You do not need to complete every optional field to record a check.

sections.title: Understand what the counts mean
paragraphs: Clear, better than usual, usual and worse than usual count as recorded checks. Unknown is counted separately. A blank or unmarked row is separate again. Clear means you recorded a clear observation at the check; it does not mean an entire unobserved day was symptom-free.

In the fictional example, week one has five recorded checks and two unknowns. Week two has six recorded checks and one unknown. Those different denominators belong in any comparison. A missed check must not be converted into a zero-symptom score.

sections.title: Choose a format for the task
paragraphs: Use the printable version when a short paper record is easier. Use the spreadsheet when editing rows and reviewing counts is useful. If importing the XLSX into another spreadsheet application, check that status lists and formulas behave as expected before relying on a summary.

The download is an Excel-format workbook, not a hosted Google Sheet. Use your own account’s import process if you prefer Sheets. Before sending a report, review its contents, remove fields you do not intend to share and use the recipient’s preferred method.

sections.title: The first conversation is about the pattern
paragraphs: The clinician may ask when it started, whether symptoms clear between episodes and whether you feel blocked on one side or both. Changes in smell, facial pressure, mucus and the effect on sleep are worth describing in your own words. A line such as “the left side feels more blocked most mornings and I stopped smelling my coffee last month” gives the clinician a place to start. Add a date range when you know one.

You may be asked what you’ve already used, how long you used it and what you remember changing. If the product name is hard to recall, a photo of the label or your medication list can help. Tell the clinician about relevant previous surgery, tests and conditions. See how to prepare for your ENT appointment for a fuller checklist.

When the timeline is hard to reconstruct, a few dated notes can do the remembering for you. AirBloom is being built to keep those check-ins and routine entries in one history, so you can find a typical day and an unusually difficult one before the visit.

sections.title: The examination and a possible nasal scope
paragraphs: An in-person examination may start with looking at the front of your nose. Nasal endoscopy lets the clinician look farther inside with a thin instrument carrying a light and a camera or viewing system. Ask them to explain what they’re looking for and what you might feel. Some clinics use a spray beforehand depending on the procedure and the patient. Tell the clinician about relevant allergies or if you’re worried about discomfort, and agree how you’ll signal for a pause. ENT UK on flexible nasal endoscopy · Cleveland Clinic on nasal endoscopy

A CT scan is a separate decision. If imaging comes up, ask what question it would answer and whether you’ll need a separate appointment. The adult sinusitis guideline distinguishes routine imaging for acute symptoms from testing used to help confirm chronic disease. Which checks are appropriate depends on your history and the clinician’s findings.

sections.title: Two ways a first visit might go
paragraphs: With a scope. Sam describes several months of blockage and a change in smell. After talking and looking at the front of the nose, the clinician explains that a scope may give a better view and asks for consent. Afterwards they discuss what they saw and when to review the plan.

Without a scope. Alex’s first appointment is by video. The clinician reviews the timeline and existing treatments, then explains what they’d like to assess at a later in-person visit. Alex leaves knowing what to bring and who will arrange the follow-up. These examples illustrate possible sequences. Your clinic’s instructions tell you what to expect locally.

sections.title: Before you leave
paragraphs: Try to leave with three things written down: the next step, who owns it and when you should hear more. If a plan includes using a medicine, ask for clear written instructions. If a decision is pending, ask what information is still needed. A one-page symptom summary can give both of you a shared record of the dates and questions that brought you in.

sources.title: ENT UK on flexible nasal endoscopy

title: What happens at your first ENT visit for sinus symptoms
answer: At a first ENT appointment for sinus problems, the clinician usually asks about your symptoms and what you’ve tried, examines your nose and discusses what should happen next. In an in-person visit, they may offer a closer look with a thin nasal scope. Some appointments end with a plan or follow-up and no scope or scan that day.

sections.title: Copy this one-page summary
paragraphs: The NHS guide to preparing questions for an appointment recommends bringing notes about what you want to discuss and a list of medicines. Use the full-size print sheet if you’d rather fill the summary in by hand.

tables.caption: Copy this one-page summary
rows: The one thing I want help understanding or managing
Start and end date, with days logged out of days in the period
What changed, when, where and whether it returned to my usual
A concrete example from sleep, work, exercise or everyday life
Product or routine, date or frequency as recorded, what I noticed
One or two decisions or next steps I want to discuss

sections.title: From scattered notes to a visit summary
paragraphs: Here are two fictional weeks from the same diary. The entries cover mornings only. “Worse” is the writer’s own comparison with their usual level of blockage.
Here is how the same notes could read on the finished page.
Why I booked. I’d like help understanding the recent increase in morning blockage.
Dates and coverage. 7–20 September. I recorded 11 of 14 mornings.

Main pattern. Blockage was worse than my usual on 2 of 5 recorded mornings in the first week and 4 of 6 in the second. Three second-week entries mentioned the left side felt more blocked. I’m unsure what happened on the three missed mornings.
Daily impact. I woke overnight on 10 September and wrote that I felt tired at work the next day.
What I used. I wrote down a saline rinse on 9 and 16 September. I felt clearer after the first entry. I didn’t record a follow-up after the second.
My questions. What would you look at to understand why it’s often worse on the left? What should I keep recording before we review it?

tables.caption: From scattered notes to a visit summary
rows: Worse on 2 of 5. One entry mentions waking overnight. Two mornings unrecorded.
Worse on 4 of 6. Three entries describe more blockage on the left. One morning unrecorded.

sections.title: Keep the dates and the uncertainty
paragraphs: If you recorded on your worst days, say so. “I only logged when it bothered me” helps the clinician interpret the entries. If your recollection reaches farther back than your diary, keep the two time frames separate: “I remember this starting around May. My dated notes begin in September.” You can use dates for visits, tests or treatments as anchors without trying to fill in everything between them.

AirBloom is being built to keep symptoms and routine logs on a dated timeline. That could make it easier to pull out the entries behind your summary when someone asks when a change began or what you were using at the time.

sections.title: Give the page a job in the room
paragraphs: Hand it over early or read the first two lines aloud if that feels easier. Put the question that matters most at the top so you can reach it even if time is short. Leave a little room to write down what the clinician wants to check and how you’ll follow up. If you’re starting with loose notes, the seven-day sinus symptom diary has space to capture the details this summary uses.

sections.title: Compare two weeks without hiding missing entries
paragraphs: Compare recorded days with recorded days, and report missing checks separately. Use clear, usual and worse-than-usual labels consistently. A week with more recorded worse days is not automatically worse overall when the number of completed checks also changed.

sections.title: Count the coverage before comparing symptoms
paragraphs: The fictional workbook contains fourteen planned checks, seven in each week. In week one, five checks were recorded and two were marked unknown. In week two, six were recorded and one was unknown. Neither week has an unmarked row. Unknown means that the check was missed or could not be described; it is not a clear day.

sections.title: Write a cautious comparison
paragraphs: A useful summary is: “I recorded five of seven checks in the first week and six of seven in the second. Worse-than-usual observations were more frequent among the checks I completed in week two. I cannot describe the three unknown checks, and this comparison does not establish a cause.”

Add daily impact in concrete terms, such as a work break or an interrupted walk, without turning those events into a validated score. Do not compare a morning-only week with a mixed morning-and-evening week as though the sampling were identical.

sections.title: Carry the uncertainty into the visit summary
paragraphs: Put the date range, coverage counts, main change and one question onto the one-page report. Keep the original diary available if the clinician wants more detail. One short comparison is easier to discuss than an unexplained total or a percentage with no denominator.

If some entries were recalled later, say so. Use the blank diary for the next period and keep its field order and labels consistent. The summary helps explain what was recorded; it does not establish that a routine or exposure caused the difference.

title: How to summarise sinus symptoms for your doctor on one page
answer: Start your sinus symptom summary with the dates you tracked, how many days you actually logged and the change you most want to discuss. Add one example of the impact, a short list of what you used and one or two questions. Take the underlying diary if you want to be able to look up a date in the room.
seoTitle: Sinus Symptom Summary for Your Doctor | Template
description: Turn your sinus diary into a one-page summary with dates, days logged, changes, daily impact and questions. Includes a blank and worked example.

sections.title: Separate the sensation from the explanation
paragraphs: “Sinus pressure” is a common way to describe fullness, pain or pressure around the cheeks, eyes or forehead. The location is a useful observation. It can be difficult to identify the source from the sensation alone. If your notes also mention light sensitivity, nausea or a headache that stops you doing things, include those details when you seek advice. Migraine can include facial discomfort and nasal symptoms. Cleveland Clinic on sinus pressure · American Migraine Foundation on sinus headache

A rainy day can involve changes in temperature, humidity and how much time you spend outside. The NHS guide to non-allergic rhinitis includes weather changes such as temperature or humidity among possible contributors to nasal symptoms. That is a separate question from whether a routine change in air pressure injured or inflamed a sinus. The published analysis above looked at what websites claimed. It did not follow people through changes in the weather.

A 2026 study of clinic patients in Charlottesville, Virginia found that worse self-reported nasal and sinus symptoms were more common on certain cold, dry or changing-weather days. The researchers compared weather types, which combine factors such as temperature, humidity and pressure. The study can speak to patterns in that group. It leaves open whether pressure alone explains what one person felt. Study on climate and sinonasal symptoms

sections.title: Compare ordinary days as well as difficult ones
paragraphs: Choose one weather source and a station near the place where you spent most of your day. If you can access hourly records, write down a pressure reading at the same local time each day, using the same unit. You might also note the change from the previous morning. Keep the source, station and time zone at the top of the sheet. Label a forecast as a forecast if you’re using it in place of a past observation.

Keep a symptom check-in even on a day when you feel fine. Write down the approximate onset if pressure starts later, where it is and what else you noticed. The table below is fictional. The numbers show how to read a small set of notes, not a pressure threshold.

Monday is the sort of day you might remember. Tuesday is just as informative because a similar drop came with no facial pressure. Wednesday shows that pressure can appear on a day with little change in this particular reading. Friday can’t tell you how you felt. Keeping all four kinds of entry makes the comparison more useful than collecting examples that fit the pattern.

When you compare a second week, use the same unit and time. If you change stations, note where and when. When a pattern looks stronger on a particular kind of day, write down what else the entries share, such as very cold mornings or a change in routine. That gives you a better account of what happened and where you still have questions.

tables.caption: Compare ordinary days as well as difficult ones
rows: Nose felt more blocked than usual

sections.title: Bring the question you still have
paragraphs: “If I bring a few dated examples, can we talk about what might explain the facial pressure?” is a more useful starting question than arriving with a cause already attached. Include where it hurt, what happened to your nose or sense of smell at the same time and whether you felt well between episodes. If flights or dives reliably bring on severe pressure, mention those separately. Clinical overview of barosinusitis

The AirBloom app is being built to place symptom check-ins and available local weather in the same history. Seeing the dates together can save a second search through weather records and give you something specific to review, including the days that go against your first impression.

If you’re trying to understand variation across several parts of your routine, see why sinus symptoms change day to day. If facial pressure is recurring or worsening, you can ask for medical advice while you’re still collecting notes. NHS sinusitis guidance

title: Does barometric pressure affect your sinuses
answer: Facial pressure can seem to follow a change in the weather. Evidence that ordinary changes in barometric pressure directly cause sinus inflammation is limited. Rapid pressure changes during flying or diving are a different situation and can cause sinus barotrauma. If facial pressure keeps returning, note what you feel and when it happens so a clinician can consider sinus and headache-related causes.

description: See what research says about weather and sinus pressure, how flying differs, and how to compare your symptom notes with local weather.

sections.title: Use two check-ins on the same morning
paragraphs: The second check-in is a practical comparison point. If you only remember at lunchtime, note the time you actually checked. Keep using any treatment according to your existing instructions. Write down if you used a spray, took a shower or left the house between check-ins so the two entries make sense later.

Example. At 07:10, Mia writes “left side more blocked, sneezed twice, no itchy eyes”. At 07:55, she writes “both sides clearer after I got up and showered”. On Saturday she follows the same check-in format and feels clear both times. That Saturday is useful even though she had nothing uncomfortable to report. It gives her a morning to compare with the others.

tables.caption: Use two check-ins on the same morning
rows: The time, which side feels blocked, how much it bothers you and whether you notice sneezing, itching, watery eyes or a runny nose
Better, the same or worse. Include which side is blocked now and what happened between entries.
Whether you were already blocked before sleep, and anything different about where you slept

sections.title: What might explain morning nasal congestion
paragraphs: Allergic rhinitis. A blocked or runny nose alongside sneezing, an itchy nose or watery eyes can be part of an allergy pattern. Dust mites, pet dander, mould and pollen are possible allergens. A morning pattern can be a reason to mention your bedroom environment or where else it happens. It takes more information to work out whether an allergy is involved. NHS allergic rhinitis · Cleveland Clinic on morning allergies

Non-allergic rhinitis. The inside of the nose can become irritated for other reasons. The NHS lists changes in temperature or humidity and irritants such as smoke or perfume. Note a change you actually remember, for example sleeping in a room that was unusually warm, instead of trying to track every possible exposure. NHS non-allergic rhinitis

The pattern matters more than the first guess. If the same side tends to stay blocked, your sense of smell has changed, or you’re also getting facial pressure or other symptoms, mention those details when you ask for advice. If you use a decongestant nasal spray, check the leaflet and tell a pharmacist how long you’ve used it. Longer-than-advised use can make stuffiness worse. NHS sinusitis · NHS decongestant guidance

sections.title: What to look for across three mornings
paragraphs: If you had a cold, a night away or a change in your usual schedule, keep that entry with a short context note. It may explain why one morning is hard to compare. The aim is a set of examples you can describe accurately when someone asks about your symptoms.

tables.caption: What to look for across three mornings
rows: Blockage was clearer at the second check-in each time
How soon it improved and what you did in between
It only happened in one place
Where you slept and how long you stayed there
It stayed mainly on one side at both check-ins
Which side, how often and when you first noticed it

sections.title: Decide what to take from the notes
paragraphs: After several mornings, look for two things: whether the blocked feeling usually changes after you get up, and whether there’s a morning that looks different. “Usually clearer by breakfast, but still blocked at lunch twice this week” is enough detail to start a conversation. If the blockage regularly begins as soon as you lie down, record that time separately. The waking check-in can show whether the feeling continued into the next morning.

AirBloom is being built around a morning symptom check-in and a dated history. If you tend to forget how yesterday started, keeping a short follow-up note beside the morning entry can help you compare the two.

If symptoms regularly affect your sleep or everyday life, are getting worse, or you’re unsure what’s causing them, ask a pharmacist or healthcare professional for advice. Take your notes if you have them. The printable sinus diary gives you somewhere to keep the morning pattern alongside smell changes and other symptoms. NHS allergic rhinitis guidance

title: Waking up with a stuffy nose every morning
answer: If you wake up with a stuffy nose most mornings, check how it feels when you first wake and again 30 to 60 minutes after getting up. A blocked nose that clears soon after waking is a different pattern to describe from one that lasts through breakfast and into the afternoon. Allergic and non-allergic rhinitis are two possibilities. The timing alone is too little information to tell them apart.

description: Compare how your nose feels on waking and 30 to 60 minutes after getting up. See which details are useful to share with a clinician.

sections.title: Copy the nasal spray log
paragraphs: Start with the name on the label, especially if you use more than one spray. The plan column is for instructions you already have. If a product is used as needed, write “as needed” or leave the planned time blank. If you record a use late, use an approximate time or note that you remember using it but can’t place when.

Use “used”, “not used” or “unsure” for the status. A reminder can tell you when you intended to do something. Mark “used” when you actually recall doing it. If you’re unsure whether you used a medicine or what to do after a missed use, follow the patient leaflet or ask a pharmacist. Medicine instructions vary by product. NHS example of product-specific instructions

tables.caption: Copy the nasal spray log

sections.title: Two entries that answer different questions
paragraphs: On 7 September there’s an approximate use time and two observations. On 8 September there’s a symptom note and an uncertain use. Both can stay in the log. Keep the second day out of any comparison that needs confirmed use, and keep the lunchtime note if you’re describing how the day felt.

tables.caption: Two entries that answer different questions
rows: Blocked before use. At noon, felt clearer.
More blocked by lunchtime. No before-check.

sections.title: Add a follow-up you can stick to
paragraphs: If you want to see what changed, pick one thing to check: how blocked you feel, how comfortable your nose feels or whether you notice irritation. Record the time of the follow-up. “Less blocked at 12:00” gives more context than “worked”. Sometimes you’ll only remember how you felt afterwards. Mark the earlier state “not recorded”. One observation can guide a question for your pharmacist or clinician.

Keep spray and rinse entries separate even if they happen a few minutes apart. The rinse worksheet has space for the device or product and a before-and-after observation. If you’re using both under an existing plan, keep following those instructions for sequence and use.

sections.title: Bring a short note if you want advice
paragraphs: If a spray feels uncomfortable or you’re unsure how you’re using it, record the name, roughly when you used it, what you noticed and whether it happened again. Take the label or a photo if you can. A useful question is “Could you check the instructions and show me how to use this product?” The print worksheet includes a small handoff card for this conversation. Use the product leaflet or ask a pharmacist or clinician about unexpected or troublesome effects. NHS medicines information

AirBloom is being built to keep reminders for your existing routine and the entries you actually log in one place. The planned follow-up note gives you somewhere to put “felt clearer later” without having to remember which use it followed.

sections.title: Keep the routine and the record separate
paragraphs: A reminder helps you remember an intention. A log helps you reconstruct what happened. If you mainly need the first, see how to remember your sinus medication routine. If you’re preparing for a visit, copy the product names and the most relevant observations into your one-page sinus symptom summary. Keep the detailed log in case you’re asked about a particular date.

sections.title: What to record after a saline nasal rinse
paragraphs: For a saline nasal rinse log, write down when you rinsed, the device or product you used and how your nose felt before and afterwards. Put the time next to the later observation. If you forgot the earlier check, mark it “not recorded” and keep the rest of the entry.

sections.title: What to record
paragraphs: Use distilled or sterile water, or tap water that has been boiled and cooled, when preparing a nasal rinse. Follow the device instructions for preparation and cleaning and follow your clinician’s instructions if you’ve been given them. The CDC’s rinse safety guide and the FDA’s device guidance explain safe water and device care.

sections.title: Copy a row for each rinse you want to record
paragraphs: In the first fictional entry, the writer recorded one observation after rinsing. Without an earlier check, the writer can say “right side felt clear at 20:15”. How much it changed is unknown. In the second example, they can say what they noticed at two points in time. Keep “about the same” if that’s what you felt. It helps make the log representative of your everyday routine.

tables.caption: Copy a row for each rinse you want to record

sections.title: Keep any discomfort in your own words
paragraphs: If you felt stinging, pressure or another unexpected sensation, note when it started, where you felt it and whether it persisted. If you have questions, take that line and the product or device name to your pharmacist or clinician. If you develop a headache, fever, confusion or vomiting after rinsing your nose, the CDC advises seeking medical attention right away.

Keep this worksheet next to your nasal spray entries so you can review the sequence. If the routine came from your clinic, check its written instructions for any questions about what to use or when. ENT UK’s saline rinse information

sections.title: How to track what changed after your usual nasal spray
paragraphs: Compare the same symptom before and after you use your usual nasal spray. Write down the actual use time and the time you next noticed the symptom. If the earlier check is missing, keep the later note and mark the starting point as unknown.

sections.title: Keep the observation matched
paragraphs: On Monday you can describe what changed and mention the shower. Wednesday gives you a later observation with no comparison point. Friday adds an example where the symptom felt about the same. Keep all three when describing the week, and keep Wednesday out of a count of matched before-and-after checks.

Try asking yourself the same question both times. “How blocked does my left side feel?” gives you a comparison you can follow. If you forget until evening, write when you checked. Products vary in when people might notice a change. Follow your own instructions, and ask a pharmacist or clinician which changes are worth monitoring for your particular spray. NHS fluticasone information · Royal Brompton and Harefield hospitals

If you ask for advice, take the product name and a short run of entries, including a day when little changed. “How should I judge whether this routine is helping?” gives the pharmacist or clinician a question they can answer with you.

tables.caption: Keep the observation matched
rows: Took a warm shower at about 09:00

sections.title: What to write down if a nasal spray feels uncomfortable
paragraphs: Write the name on the nasal spray label, when you used it, what you felt and when it began. Include what your nose felt like beforehand and any other products you used around the same time. A pharmacist can use those details to check the leaflet and talk through what happened.

sections.title: What to record
paragraphs: Get emergency help if you have trouble breathing or sudden swelling of your lips, tongue or throat after using a medicine. In the UK, call 999. If you feel unwell or are unsure what to do about a symptom, use the product leaflet or seek advice from a pharmacist or clinician. NHS anaphylaxis guidance · NHS example of product-specific side effects

sections.title: Copy this pharmacist handoff card
paragraphs: A fictional example might read: “Used Spray A at about 08:00. My nose already felt dry. Noticed stinging in the left nostril soon afterwards and it had eased by breakfast. I used a saline mist earlier, exact time unknown.” Bring the box or a clear photo if you can.
If you weren’t sure whether you used a product, write “unsure”. Keep that uncertainty when you describe the order. Check the leaflet or ask a pharmacist about unexpected or troublesome effects.

Date, actual time and anything you remember about how you used it
What you noticed beforehand, what changed and how long it lasted
Other sprays or rinses used around the same time
What you want checked, such as the leaflet instructions or technique

sections.title: Copy the pollen symptom diary
paragraphs: At the top of your sheet, write the source, area or station, and whether it’s a forecast or a measured count. If you travel, note where you spent the day. Record the type of pollen if the provider breaks it out, and copy the provider’s units or categories as shown.

For UK forecasts, start with the Met Office pollen forecast. In the US, the American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology explains pollen counts and links to monitoring resources. Check the coverage for your area and how often the station posts an update. If nothing is available for that date, write “no local reading”.

tables.caption: Copy the pollen symptom diary

sections.title: See what a week can and can’t tell you
paragraphs: This is a fictional example using one regional provider’s categories. The symptoms are the writer’s own observations.

On Monday and Tuesday, the forecast category was the same and the days looked different. The different time outdoors is a detail worth keeping. Wednesday is the row you might forget if you only looked up pollen after a sneezy afternoon. Thursday and Friday each have a different missing piece. Keep both so a blank never turns into “low pollen” or “felt fine”.

Blocked nose in the morning, before going outside

sections.title: Record the symptoms you actually noticed
paragraphs: You can write “eyes itchy, sneezing, no blockage” instead of giving the whole day one score. Include when symptoms appeared, especially if they started before you went outside. If you used a medicine you already take, note when you used it as context. Pollen can cause hay fever, and the NHS guide to allergic rhinitis also lists other possible allergens, including dust mites, animal dander and mould. Use your diary to describe what happened and when you want to ask about it.

AirBloom is being built to put available local pollen and symptom check-ins in one view. Your own note about where you spent the afternoon is still worth keeping. A city-level reading can give you the day’s context while your notes describe the places you actually went.

sections.title: What if your provider only shows a daily category
paragraphs: Write “high forecast” or “low forecast” exactly as the provider displays it. You can still compare your own entries across those days. If you switch to a provider that reports a measured count, start a new set of comparisons and write the units at the top. Keep tree, grass and weed pollen in separate fields if your source distinguishes them.

sections.title: Compare like with like
paragraphs: Look for dates with the same provider, area and pollen type, then compare symptoms and time outdoors. Keep a day with a high forecast and few symptoms and a day with a low forecast and more symptoms if both occurred. If a change keeps showing up, bring two or three dates to a pharmacist or healthcare professional, especially if symptoms are worsening or affecting sleep or everyday life. For other kinds of daily variation, see why sinus symptoms change day to day. NHS allergic rhinitis guidance

answer: Use a pollen symptom diary to record the local pollen level, where and how long you were outside, and the symptoms you noticed. Use the same provider when comparing days, and keep low-pollen days, clear days and missed check-ins in the record. A regional forecast gives context for your notes. Your own exposure can vary within that area.

sections.title: Try the same three entries in each format
paragraphs: Use sample details first. Add a clear day, a worse day and a missed day. Then find the worse day and add what happened to your sleep. Finally, see what you could hand a clinician. It might be a printed sheet, a short summary or an export you can open yourself.

Check whether the output makes it clear which days you recorded. If the export shows a number without the note you typed or makes the missed day look clear, see whether another view keeps those details. If you plan to use a shared document or device, check who can access it before entering real symptoms. A quick privacy check is to find where the service explains what it stores, who it shares data with and how deletion works.

AirBloom is being built around short sinus check-ins and a history of symptoms and routines. If you mainly need a page you can use at your next visit, start with the seven-day printable diary and try the same three-entry test there.

sections.title: Pick the format you can come back to
paragraphs: A few dated entries are enough to see whether you can keep up the habit. If typing on a phone feels fiddly on rough days, try a shorter daily note. You can always turn the details you did capture into a one-page symptom summary.

title: How to choose a way to track sinus symptoms
answer: Choose the simplest way to keep a dated sinus symptom record you can use again. If paper is easiest to keep by the bed, start there. A spreadsheet makes it easier to sort dates. An app may suit you if reminders and looking back on a phone are part of the job.
description: Compare paper, spreadsheets and phone apps for recording sinus symptoms, keeping missing entries visible and preparing a record for your next visit.

sections.title: What to record
paragraphs: Get emergency help for a sudden, extremely painful headache or a headache with new weakness, speech difficulty or loss of vision. In the UK, call 999 or go to A&E. If headaches keep returning, arrange a GP or clinician appointment. NHS headache guidance

sections.title: What to put on your headache note card
paragraphs: Use the printable headache note card to keep several entries together. Record what you noticed before the headache as well as during it. “Had a blocked nose since Sunday” is a different detail from “right nostril felt blocked an hour into the headache”. If you only remember noticing the symptoms together, write that. The times are useful even when they’re approximate.

tables.caption: What to put on your headache note card
rows: Date, first symptom, what appeared next, and when each settled
Side, location and words such as pressure, throbbing or ache
Blockage, discharge, watery eyes or a change in smell, with times when known
Light or sound sensitivity, nausea, recent cold symptoms, or anything else you noticed
What it interrupted, anything you took as part of your usual plan, and the time you took it

sections.title: How the clues can overlap
paragraphs: People sometimes expect a stuffy nose to point only to the sinuses. The American Migraine Foundation describes congestion, a runny nose and watery eyes as features that can accompany migraine. It also describes nausea and sensitivity to light or sound as useful details to report. The Mayo Clinic notes that sinus-related pain can accompany thick nasal discharge or a reduced sense of smell. These are observations to share with a clinician, especially when several appear together. American Migraine Foundation · Mayo Clinic

This person could tell a clinician: “The ache came first, the stuffiness started later, and the light bothered me enough that I stopped work.” If the next episode starts during a cold or leaves the nose blocked after the pain has gone, keep that example too. It gives the clinician a second sequence to compare. A diary can help you recall each episode and how it affected your day. NHS headache guidance

If your nose notes and headache notes usually live in different places, AirBloom is being built to keep the symptoms you choose to record in a dated history. It can give you one place to look for the day’s sequence before an appointment.

tables.caption: How the clues can overlap
rows: Ache near the left brow. Nose felt clear.
Left side of nose felt blocked. Light from the window bothered me.
Still had the headache. Stopped work and sat in a quieter room.
Pain had eased. Nose felt about normal again.
No headache at check-in. Unsure exactly when it ended.

sections.title: Note which symptoms outlasted the pain
paragraphs: If the pain stopped on Tuesday but your nose stayed blocked until Friday, record both end dates. If you had three headaches during one week of congestion, give the headaches separate rows and use one line for the nasal symptoms that ran through the week. That keeps the longer stretch visible. It also gives your clinician a way to ask which symptoms usually travel together.
Use “last noticed” or “gone by” if you can’t pin down an end time. Keep the end time approximate when you only remember the next check.

sections.title: Bring two examples and one question
paragraphs: Choose one typical episode and another that felt different. Add a count if you have one, such as “three episodes over the last month, two with a clear start time”. Tell the clinician if you only wrote down the worst days. A question to start with is “What parts of this pattern would help you decide what to check next?” For a related pattern, see facial pressure without a blocked nose.

title: Sinus headache or migraine and what to track
answer: When a headache comes with facial pressure, a stuffy nose or watery eyes, record the head and nose symptoms on the same timeline. Migraine can include nasal symptoms. Sinusitis can also involve facial discomfort, especially when it occurs with other nasal symptoms. Tell your clinician what started first, how long each symptom lasted and whether they cleared together.
seoTitle: Sinus Headache or Migraine? What to Track
description: Track headache and nasal symptoms on the same timeline. Use the printable note card to record onset, duration and what to tell your clinician.

sections.title: Record three moments around bedtime
paragraphs: The printable position card has space for all three moments. The second moment can be whenever you naturally notice a change. “Left side more blocked a few minutes after I lay down” is enough. If you did not check later, leave that box blank or mark it “not recorded”. There is no need to set an alarm or repeat a position that feels uncomfortable.

rows: Time and room. Is your nose already blocked? Which side?
Approximate time. Is it the same, worse or clearer? Which side now?
What changed when you sat or stood up? If you only noticed in the morning, record that time.

sections.title: Why it can feel different after lying down
paragraphs: A change in position can affect how congested your nose feels. If you notice it within minutes of lying down, tell your clinician whether it varies by side and whether it eases when you’re upright. Also note if the nose already felt blocked while you were sitting. A stuffy nose that starts before bed can still become more noticeable once you settle. Henry Ford Health

The room can be part of the picture. Dust mites, pet dander and mould can contribute to allergic rhinitis. The NHS also lists temperature changes and irritants such as smoke or perfume as possible contributors to non-allergic rhinitis. If it happens while you sit in the bedroom as well as after you lie down, keep both observations. If you already spent a night elsewhere, that gives you another day to compare. NHS allergic rhinitis · NHS non-allergic rhinitis

sections.title: Use a second check in the same room
paragraphs: If you happen to sit in the bedroom before lying down, record how your nose feels there. That gives you a comparison with fewer changes at once. On a night when you go directly from the sofa to bed, you’ve changed the room and your position. Note both. The record can still show when the stuffiness became noticeable.

If one side feels more blocked, write which side and how you were lying at the time. Record a later change of side only if you noticed one. You can leave nights with no follow-up as unknown. A note that says “left side blocked at 22:20, no later check” still tells you when you first noticed the change.

sections.title: A fictional comparison over three nights
paragraphs: Monday suggests a position-linked observation worth mentioning. Tuesday starts earlier and leaves an overnight gap. Saturday gives you a comparison, but the room and evening routine were both different. You could say “two blocked evenings at home, one clear evening away” and give the details when asked.

If your notes end up scattered across bedtime and morning, AirBloom is being built to show symptom entries alongside optional sleep context. Keep the before-bed and later observations separate so you can see when the change started.

After a few nights, count the times you actually checked before and after lying down. If it changed on two of three paired checks, say that. Keep the nights when you only noticed on waking in a separate group. That gives a clearer answer if a clinician asks when the blockage usually starts.

sections.title: When to ask for advice
paragraphs: Ask a pharmacist or clinician if the pattern persists, disrupts sleep or affects daily life. Mention if the same side stays blocked or if you’ve also noticed changes in smell or recurring facial pain. If the problem only shows up on waking, try the morning nasal congestion check-in. If you have several symptoms to record, use the printable sinus diary. NHS allergic rhinitis · NHS sinusitis

title: Why your nose feels stuffy when you lie down
answer: If your nose feels stuffy after you lie down, the timing can help you describe the pattern. Note whether you were already blocked while sitting up, what happens once you settle and what changes when you next get up. Lying down can make congestion more noticeable, and room exposures or an existing nasal problem may also contribute.
seoTitle: Stuffy Nose When Lying Down? What to Track
description: Compare how your nose feels before lying down, after settling and after getting up. Includes a three-moment card and worked example.

sections.title: Three timelines with a similar starting symptom
paragraphs: Each person below has a stuffy nose. These fictional timelines show what is worth describing in a consultation.

Timing helps a clinician understand the story. It can’t show what caused the symptoms. A person can have an allergy pattern and also develop sinus symptoms during a cold. A regional pollen forecast gives useful context for the first timeline if available. It cannot tell you what that person breathed. AAAAI comparison of colds, allergies and sinusitis

sections.title: Make a five-field note
paragraphs: 1. Start. Write when you first noticed the change. An approximate date is fine. If you already had some blockage before that day, put your usual symptoms on a separate line.
2. Sequence. Write what came first and what appeared later. Separate a newly blocked nose from a new pressure sensation in a nose that’s often blocked.
3. Context. Note a recent cold, where you were or a specific exposure you remember. A phrase such as “cleaned the spare room” is useful even if you have no idea whether it mattered.
4. Clear days and gaps. Say when you felt better, whether symptoms fully cleared, and when you simply didn’t check. If the dates are fuzzy, write “cleared sometime before Monday” or “uncertain”.
5. Impact and next question. Note what was harder than usual, such as sleeping through the night, and write one question you’d like help answering.

sections.title: Where to put pollen and routine notes
paragraphs: Keep pollen, products you used and changes in your environment beside the dates they belong to. If a day felt better after several things changed, write them down in the order you remember. You can bring that sequence to a pharmacist or clinician. The pollen symptom diary has fields for region, provider and time outdoors.

AirBloom is being built to put daily symptom entries and available local conditions in one view. That gives you one place to find the days you want to talk through, while keeping your observations separate from the forecast.

sections.title: When to ask for help
paragraphs: Ask a pharmacist or GP if you’re unsure what’s causing recurring symptoms or if they regularly affect sleep or everyday life. Seek advice sooner if sinus symptoms worsen or you feel very unwell. The NHS sinusitis guide and NHS allergic rhinitis guide explain when to get help. If you’ve already got dated entries, bring a one-page summary.

title: Sinusitis or allergies and what to track before a visit
answer: Start with when your symptoms appeared and what happened next. Sneezing and itchy eyes that recur around a particular exposure can fit allergic rhinitis. Blockage and facial discomfort that develop during or after a cold can fit sinusitis. The symptoms can overlap, so bring a timeline of what you noticed instead of choosing a label for it.
seoTitle: Sinusitis or Allergies? What to Track Before a Visit
description: Compare three symptom timelines and use five fields to record onset, context, clear days and impact before a visit.

sections.title: What to record
paragraphs: Get medical help immediately if you develop a headache, fever, confusion or vomiting after nasal rinsing. The CDC lists these as signs to act on promptly. CDC guidance on when immediate care is needed

sections.title: Check the water label before you mix
paragraphs: A saline packet is for preparing the solution according to the instructions. Start with safe water. If you buy a ready-to-use sterile saline product labelled for nasal use, follow its label. Ask a pharmacist or your clinician if you are unsure which product or directions apply to your device. FDA rinse device guidance

sections.title: Keep the instructions where you rinse
paragraphs: Keep your device instructions and the water label handy. Follow the directions for cleaning and drying the device, and any clinic instructions if the rinse was recommended for you. If someone else brings a bottle home, read the label before opening it so you know which type you have. FDA rinse device guidance

For a routine you already follow, AirBloom is being built to help you log when you rinsed and how you felt later. Use the official guidance for water and device care and the nasal routine log for observations you want to remember.

title: What water is safe for a nasal rinse
answer: Use store-bought water labelled distilled or sterile, or tap water that has been boiled and allowed to cool, to prepare a nasal rinse. The CDC and FDA advise using water prepared for this purpose because water that is safe to drink may contain germs that can cause a serious infection if it gets into the nose.
seoTitle: What Water Is Safe for a Nasal Rinse?
description: Check which water labels are suitable for nasal rinsing and where to find CDC and FDA instructions on preparation and device care.

sections.title: What persistent symptoms can look like
paragraphs: Your nose may feel blocked most days. Mucus may drain through the nose or down the throat. You might notice that foods or coffee smell different, or that a feeling of fullness in your face comes and goes. The adult guideline describes chronic rhinosinusitis as a pattern of at least two of the main symptoms along with evidence of inflammation. The symptoms can overlap with other conditions. AAO-HNS adult sinusitis guideline

When you look back, separate the symptoms that stayed from the ones that flared. “Pressure was worse for one week, but my nose was partly blocked throughout” is a different story from “everything cleared between the difficult weeks”. The distinction is worth making even when some dates are approximate.

sections.title: Turn several months into a short timeline
paragraphs: A short description might read: “Blocked most mornings since around mid-January. Smell seemed reduced from February. The pressure eased in March, but the blockage stayed. I’m unsure about the travel days.” This lets the clinician ask about the earliest change and any days when symptoms genuinely cleared.

sections.title: Why the clinician may want a closer look
paragraphs: The examination can help check whether there are signs of inflammation or another explanation for the symptoms. The adult guideline describes looking inside the nose, nasal endoscopy or CT as ways to document inflammation, depending on the case. A clinician may choose which approach makes sense after hearing the history and examining you. AAO-HNS summary of guideline actions

If a scope or scan is discussed, ask what it would help them check and what happens after the result. If a test has already been done, bring the date and report if you have it. The first ENT appointment guide walks through what may happen during a visit.

sections.title: Put an approximate start on the page
paragraphs: A calendar can give you an anchor. Perhaps you noticed the smell change around a particular trip or remember mentioning the blockage at an earlier appointment. Write the anchor and how sure you are. “Around the first week of February” is often enough to show which symptoms started together and which appeared later.

sections.title: What to record between visits
paragraphs: Use the same few fields most days: blockage, drainage if present, pressure, smell and what affected your day. A clear day deserves a row, too. If you’ve used a routine, write down what you used and when. If you only remember the month you began, say so. After a few weeks, you can turn the entries into a one-page summary.
AirBloom is being built to show symptom entries and routine use together over time. That can make it easier to find what stayed the same after a rough spell passed.

Arrange advice if symptoms keep coming back, are mainly on one side, or persist despite self-care. Seek help sooner if you feel very unwell or symptoms worsen. You can ask about the pattern before you’ve tracked it for 12 weeks. NHS sinusitis guidance

title: Chronic sinusitis symptoms and what clinicians check
answer: Chronic sinusitis, also called chronic rhinosinusitis, involves lasting inflammation in the nose and sinuses. In an adult assessment, clinicians look for at least 12 weeks of symptoms such as blocked nose, nasal drainage, facial pressure or reduced smell, and check for signs of inflammation. The time course and the examination both matter.
seoTitle: Chronic Sinusitis Symptoms and What Clinicians Check
description: See which persistent symptoms clinicians ask about, what an exam can check, and how to build a useful timeline for your visit.

sections.title: What to record
paragraphs: Get emergency help for facial pressure with a sudden, extremely painful headache, new weakness, speech difficulty, loss of vision. New swelling around an eye, double vision or reduced vision with possible sinusitis also needs urgent hospital assessment. NHS headache guidance · NICE acute sinusitis guidance

sections.title: Describe the pressure without assuming where it came from
paragraphs: Start with the location. “Under my left eye”, “behind both eyebrows” and “along the upper teeth on the right” are more specific than “my sinuses hurt”. Use a word that feels accurate, such as pressure, ache or stabbing, then say how long it lasted.

If you checked and your nose felt clear, record that. If you didn’t think to check, write “not recorded”. A change in smell or nasal discharge can still be worth mentioning when blockage is absent. ENT UK facial pain guide

sections.title: A worked entry you could read aloud
paragraphs: “At about 16:00 on Thursday, I felt an ache under my right cheekbone. My nose felt clear on both sides and my sense of smell seemed usual. My upper teeth felt sore while I was eating at 18:00. I noticed the pressure had eased by bedtime. I didn’t record when it stopped.”

This note gives a clinician or dentist a location and a sequence. It leaves open whether the cheek and tooth sensations were related. If the same pattern happens again, write down what was similar and what changed. If the pressure comes with headache or sensitivity to light, the headache and nasal symptom note card gives you a place to capture both.

If you keep symptom notes on your phone, AirBloom is being built to keep dated check-ins together. You could use it to find the day your face felt sore and your nose felt clear, rather than reconstructing it at the appointment.
