sections.title: Use a clear day as a comparison
paragraphs: If you have another episode, check whether the pressure comes on in the same place and whether your nose still feels clear. It can also help to keep one observation from a day when your face feels normal. If you sometimes feel pressure with a blocked nose and sometimes with a clear nose, write down an example of each. That gives the person seeing you two patterns to ask about.
Keep the words you used at the time. “A dull ache beneath the eye” may be easier to compare later than a label you added after searching online.

sections.title: When to get recurring pressure checked
paragraphs: Make an appointment if the pressure keeps returning, persists or is getting worse. If it is linked to a particular tooth or chewing, mention that when seeking dental or medical advice. Bring two examples if you have them and say whether you felt normal in between. ENT UK facial pain guide · NHS headache guidance

title: What facial pressure without a blocked nose can mean
answer: Facial pressure can occur even when your nose feels clear. The sensation alone gives limited clues about the cause. Migraine, dental problems and other conditions can cause pain around the cheek, brow or eye. Tell a clinician where you felt it, what was happening at the same time and which nasal symptoms you checked for.
seoTitle: Facial Pressure Without a Blocked Nose
description: Record where facial pressure occurs, how long it lasts and what you noticed alongside it. Includes a worked example and care signposts.

sections.title: What the two terms mean in an adult assessment
paragraphs: The guideline describes clinical definitions. Four periods of stuffiness in a diary are useful to report even when you don’t know how many were infections. A clinician can ask about the pattern of each bout and whether symptoms were entirely gone in between. For suspected chronic sinusitis, an examination, nasal endoscopy or CT can help document inflammation. AAO-HNS guideline and action statements

sections.title: Two fictional histories
paragraphs: Separate bouts. Priya recorded rough spells in January, April, August and November. Blockage and discharge cleared after each, and she wrote down several symptom-free dates. Only two spells were assessed by a clinician. She brings the dates and says that she doesn’t know whether all four spells were infections.

Symptoms stayed between worse weeks. Mark’s nose felt blocked most days from January through April. His sense of smell changed in February. He noticed pressure for several days in March. The pressure eased, while blockage remained. Some travel days have no notes. He brings the date range and describes the two symptoms that stayed.

Both histories contain difficult weeks. Priya’s notes help show the gaps between them. Mark’s notes help show what remained once the worst part passed. The gap can be the hardest thing to recall if you only ever write down symptoms on rough days.

sections.title: Copy an episode and gap row
paragraphs: Use the printable episode and gap worksheet for several stretches. Use “clear” when the symptoms you’re tracking were absent, “ongoing” when something remained and “unknown” when you missed the check or can’t remember. If symptoms partly improved, say what got better and what stayed. If you’ve already got daily rows, the sinus symptom diary guide shows how to record an episode across several dates.
AirBloom is being built to keep clear days, flare notes and missing check-ins visible on the same dated history. That can help you find a week between bouts when a clinician asks how you felt.

sections.title: Count the gaps you can describe
paragraphs: For each rough stretch, write the first date you noticed a change and the first date you remember feeling clear again. If your usual baseline includes blockage, use “back to usual, still partly blocked”. That is a useful observation when a clinician asks whether all symptoms went away.

If someone assessed a bout, add the date and what you were told if you remember. Keep your own observations in a separate line. The two details serve different purposes: one shows when you sought care, and the other shows what happened before and afterwards.

sections.title: What to ask at your appointment
paragraphs: “Did these seem like separate episodes, or does the blockage in between change what you’d check?” is a practical question to bring. Ask for medical advice if symptoms keep returning or are getting worse. Take the dates you have and leave any unknowns visible in your one-page summary. NHS sinusitis guidance

title: Recurrent sinusitis versus chronic sinusitis
answer: The useful distinction is what happens between bouts. In recurrent acute sinusitis, separate episodes clear in between. In chronic sinusitis, symptoms persist for at least 12 weeks and a clinician finds evidence of inflammation. Someone with ongoing symptoms can still have worse weeks. Record the clear stretches as carefully as the rough ones.

paragraphs: Use the source you would normally check for your area. Write whether the number was a forecast or a current or past reading. If you spent the afternoon somewhere else, record that area. If the reading was taken at a different time from your check-in, keep both times.

sections.title: Keep UK and US readings in separate columns
paragraphs: UK. The Daily Air Quality Index uses a scale of 1 to 10 and bands from low to very high. For example, 5 is moderate on that scale. If you recorded a forecast, label it as one. UK DAQI health advice

US. AirNow uses the US AQI. For example, 75 is in the moderate category on the US scale. Record the pollutant, such as fine particles, if your source shows it. Write “US AQI 75, moderate” in full if you might later read the notes alongside UK data. AirNow AQI basics
The two numbers come from different scales. For a comparison, use the same service and location where possible. Use official advice if your area issues an alert.

paragraphs: Monday and Tuesday share a forecast category, but the two days look different. Keep both. Thursday shows why air and symptoms need separate fields: one may be available when the other isn’t. The US row illustrates the format rather than adding a comparable number to the UK set.

sections.title: Match the times before you compare
paragraphs: If a reading is labelled noon but the symptom began at 07:30, keep the gap visible. A forecast made the previous evening can still be useful, as long as it stays labelled as a forecast. The printable air quality log gives you separate spaces for the reading and check-in times.

sections.title: Put smoke days in context
paragraphs: If there’s a wildfire smoke alert, follow official guidance first. Later you can add whether you were indoors or outdoors, what you noticed and which reading was available. A missed outdoor reading can stay blank. If you need current information, see the AirNow Fire and Smoke Map in the US or UK DAQI health advice and local alerts in the UK.

AirBloom is being built to show available local air quality alongside the symptoms you choose to record. Your own note about where you actually were still matters. It can distinguish a walk outside from a check-in made indoors on the same day.

If you’re also comparing pollen, use the pollen diary to keep pollen type and provider separate. After a week, pull out one day that fits your first impression and one that doesn’t. Both are worth keeping.

sections.title: How to log nasal symptoms during wildfire smoke
paragraphs: During a wildfire smoke event, follow local health and emergency advice first. When you can safely make a note, record where you were, time indoors and outdoors, what you noticed and whether an air quality reading was available. Leave missing readings marked as unknown.

sections.title: What to record
paragraphs: For US conditions, use the AirNow Fire and Smoke Map and CDC wildfire smoke guidance. In the UK, check local alerts and UK air quality health advice. If you have urgent symptoms, follow local emergency guidance and seek help before completing any diary.

The morning symptom note still has value without a number. If the smoke smell or symptoms began before you went outside, record that order if you remember.
Add the entry to the air quality diary beside an ordinary day if you want to compare them later. A gap is useful to show where your record stops.

title: How to keep an air quality and nasal symptoms diary
answer: Pair each nasal symptom check-in with the time and place you were there, the local air quality reading and what you were doing. Keep the reading and your observation in separate columns. Outdoor air quality gives context for the day. It cannot tell you how much pollution you breathed indoors or what caused your symptoms.

sections.title: Write the order you noticed things
paragraphs: Start with one evening when it happened. A note made before bed can help you remember whether your throat already felt coated. Once you settle, record the first thing you noticed, such as a need to clear your throat or a sensation of mucus. If you wake later, say whether you remember coughing before you woke or only after you were awake.
In this example, the writer can say “I noticed the mucus sensation after I lay down. I was awake before I remember coughing.” That preserves the order without attributing the awakening to the cough.

sections.title: Keep a daytime comparison
paragraphs: On another day the same person might write “throat felt coated while I was making lunch, then again on the sofa before bed”. That’s a different pattern to describe. If you notice it only after settling, write down which room you were in and what you felt first. If it also happens upright, give your clinician an example with the time and activity.

Throat clearing is something you do. The feeling of mucus is something you notice. Record either one even if the other is absent. A note such as “kept clearing my throat during a phone call, no mucus sensation recorded” can be useful. The NHS catarrh guide describes mucus sensation, cough and the need to clear the throat as symptoms people may experience.

sections.title: If you woke in the middle of it
paragraphs: Write down what you remember at the first moment you were aware. “Woke with a coated throat and coughed once” records two observations. If you share a room and someone noticed you coughing first, label that as their observation. A morning without a night entry stays unknown. There’s no need to set alarms to collect a more complete record.
AirBloom is being built to keep symptom and sleep notes in a dated history. That could make it easier to pair a note made before bed with one made the next morning.

Before an appointment, pick one night when the throat sensation started after lying down and one day when it happened upright, if you have both. Add what happened to your nose at the same time. A short note such as “clear nose on both occasions, coughing only after I woke” gives your clinician a clearer starting point.

sections.title: When to ask for help
paragraphs: If the mucus sensation or need to clear your throat lasts more than a few weeks, speak to your GP. Give an example of the nighttime order and say whether it happens during the day. If your main symptom is a blocked nose that starts when you lie down, use the bedtime congestion guide to track that separately. NHS catarrh guidance

sections.title: Postnasal drip or throat clearing: describe the timing
paragraphs: Record a mucus sensation, throat clearing, cough and waking as separate observations. Note which happened first and whether each began before or after lying down. The sequence can help you explain your experience; it cannot identify the cause.

sections.title: Which happened first?
paragraphs: “I had postnasal drip all night” can hide several experiences. You may have noticed a sensation in the throat, cleared it repeatedly, coughed, or woken before noticing any of these. Write the words that describe what you felt rather than assuming that mucus caused every event.

The NHS uses catarrh to describe a build-up of mucus and includes a frequent need to clear the throat among possible symptoms. That explanation does not establish why an individual is clearing their throat. A note about timing is information for a conversation, not a diagnosis.

sections.title: A fictional evening-to-morning sequence
paragraphs: Compare the order in this fictional example with a second evening when throat clearing started while the person was still sitting upright. The difference belongs in the record even when the bedroom and bedtime were similar. Keep the two episodes separate rather than forcing one explanation.

rows: Whether cough caused waking is unknown

sections.title: A short note for a visit
paragraphs: Write the date, the sensation in your own words, what happened first, whether it also occurred during the day, and the effect on sleep. If you missed a check, say so. Bring persistent or troublesome symptoms to a clinician and use the official NHS catarrh page for its current care guidance. Do not postpone getting advice while collecting a more complete diary.

title: Postnasal drip when lying down and what to track overnight
answer: If you feel mucus at the back of your throat after lying down, note whether it was already there while you were upright. Record the mucus sensation, throat clearing, coughing and waking as separate observations. Lying down can make the sensation more noticeable. The timing alone cannot tell you what caused it.

faqs.answer: “I had postnasal drip all night” can hide several experiences. You may have noticed a sensation in the throat, cleared it repeatedly, coughed, or woken before noticing any of these. Write the words that describe what you felt rather than assuming that mucus caused every event.

sections.title: What to record
paragraphs: Use these labels to describe where you felt the pressure.

sections.title: Mark the location in your own words
paragraphs: Point to the place on your face or use the map to find a description. Write “left brow”, “both cheeks”, “bridge of nose” or “upper teeth on the right” if that fits. Say whether it began in one spot and later spread. These labels help you describe the sensation. Several conditions can cause pain in the same area. ENT UK facial pain guide

Use a word you would actually say. Dull pressure, aching, pulsing and sharp pain are all reasonable descriptions. If the word changes across the day, describe the change. “Started as a dull ache and felt sharper by lunchtime” can be easier to discuss than a rating without any context.

sections.title: Use three sentences at the visit
paragraphs: If you first felt the pressure on waking, say that. You may not know when it began. For example: “I woke with pressure across both eyebrows at 06:40. My nose was partly blocked then, but both sides felt clearer by breakfast. I noticed the pressure again when I bent to tie my shoes.” If a night note is missing, leave the start open.

sections.title: Add the symptoms you noticed at the same time
paragraphs: Useful details can include nasal blockage or drainage, changes in smell, tooth pain, nausea or sensitivity to light. If you checked and a symptom was absent, say so. If you forgot to check, leave it unknown. A second example that felt different helps your clinician see whether the pattern is consistent. ENT UK facial pain guide · American Migraine Foundation
If it’s hard to recall the exact day in the room, AirBloom is being built to keep dated symptom check-ins together. Look back for a typical entry and copy it to the printable facial pressure card.

sections.title: Put the most important example first
paragraphs: Bring the shortest version you can read aloud. If it has happened several times, say roughly how often and whether the same side comes up. Add a question you want answered before the appointment ends. For symptoms spanning several weeks, use the one-page sinus symptom summary and keep the face card as the specific example.
If the pressure comes with a sudden, extremely painful headache, loss of vision, weakness or trouble speaking, seek emergency help. NHS headache guidance

sections.title: A waking-to-midmorning facial-pressure note
paragraphs: Describe the location, side and time of facial pressure when you wake, then record what you notice later without assuming why it changed. A location map names an area; it does not identify the condition causing a sensation.

sections.title: Record location and timing separately
paragraphs: Use the face map as a way to point to the area you mean. “Over the right cheek” is a description. It is not proof that the sinus beneath that area is the source. Record headache, nasal blockage and other symptoms in their own fields rather than placing them all under “sinus pain.”

If you first noticed the sensation after waking, write that. It does not establish whether the sensation was present during sleep. If the next check is much later, keep the gap visible instead of inventing an exact recovery time.

sections.title: A fictional morning with an unknown interval
paragraphs: In this example the later observation is different, but the two checks do not show when the change happened. A brief handoff preserves both what was noticed and what remains uncertain.

rows: Pressure over right cheek; moderate in own words

sections.title: Turn the row into three sentences
paragraphs: “I noticed pressure over my right cheek when I woke at about 7:10. It was less noticeable at 10:15, but I did not check between those times. Right nasal blockage was also present at the first check, and I would like help understanding the pattern.”

Add how the experience affected your morning and any question you want answered. Use current official care guidance when symptoms are concerning; the purpose of this worksheet is description, not reassurance or a diagnosis.

sources.title: Trigeminal Neuralgia Association: Sinusitis and facial pain

title: How to describe facial pressure to your doctor
answer: Tell your doctor where the pressure starts, which side it affects and what happens alongside it. Give one recent example with a start time, a rough duration and what you were doing. “A dull pressure under my right eye for about two hours” gives them a more specific starting point than “my sinuses hurt”.

description: Use a face map and a printable three-sentence note card to describe location, side, timing and what happened alongside the pressure.

sections.title: Use one row for both observations
paragraphs: Use a familiar, everyday example you already came across. Coffee, soap or food you were preparing might give you something you remember. Write “coffee smelled weaker”, “soap smelled different” or “I couldn’t smell breakfast”. Leave that field unknown if you didn’t notice anything specific. Do not use gas, smoke or chemicals to test your sense of smell.

sections.title: Compare blocked and clearer days
paragraphs: A useful summary is “I first noticed a change on Wednesday and it was still there on one day when my nose felt clear”. The first noticed date may be later than the actual start. If smell felt different at lunch and normal at dinner, keep both observations when you can.

tables.caption: Compare blocked and clearer days
rows: Both sides blocked after a cold
Coffee smelled faint. Unsure if the change started earlier.
Nose felt clear on both sides

sections.title: Give the GP a specific example
paragraphs: Bring the approximate onset date, any recent cold or other illness you remember, and one clearer-nose day if you have one. Describe whether smell was weaker, gone, or changed in character. Say if food also tasted different. The NHS describes several kinds of smell change and recommends seeing a GP if it hasn’t returned to normal in a few weeks. NHS smell guidance

If changes persist and you have a longer symptom history, the one-page sinus summary gives you a place to include dates and what else was happening. You can ask for advice before the record is complete.

sections.title: Capture the next time you notice a change
paragraphs: If smell starts to come back, write down what you were able to notice and when. There can be a difference between noticing one familiar smell and feeling back to your usual. Keep the original entry so you can describe both stages. If you no longer remember whether your nose was clear that day, leave it open.

sections.title: Make room for everyday safety
paragraphs: If your sense of smell is reduced or absent, you may miss warning smells from fire, leaking gas or spoiled food. Follow the NHS safety links and make sure you have ways to check those hazards without relying on smell. Keep safety checks separate from any informal smell observation.

AirBloom is being built to keep daily sinus observations together. A dated note about smell next to a blockage check-in can make it easier to see whether the changes moved together and find the examples you want to discuss.

sources.title: NHS lost or changed sense of smell

title: What to track when your sense of smell changes after congestion
answer: Track nasal blockage and smell separately. Write when each change first became noticeable and whether smell returned when your nose felt clearer. If a familiar smell seems weaker or different, name the example and the date. A timeline can help your GP understand what changed. Colds, sinusitis and allergies are among the possible causes.
seoTitle: Smell Changes After Nasal Congestion | What to Track
description: Track smell and blockage separately so you can describe when each changed and what happened on clearer days.

sections.title: Keep the first date and the direction of change
paragraphs: Write the start of the cold and the start of the sinus symptoms separately if you remember them. If there was an improvement, describe what actually got better and for how long. A note such as “pressure eased but my nose never cleared” gives more information than “relapse”.

Cold began Monday. Pressure appeared Thursday. Clearer by the second weekend, with some blockage still present.
Better for a while, then worse
Started to feel better on Friday. New or worse facial pain the following Monday.

sections.title: When to get help in the UK
paragraphs: The NHS suggests speaking to a pharmacist for sinusitis advice. It recommends seeing a GP if you haven’t improved after seven days of treatment from a pharmacy or GP, after three weeks of self-care, or if you keep getting sinusitis. Ask for urgent help through a GP or NHS 111 if you are very unwell, painkillers aren’t helping or symptoms are getting worse, or you have a weakened immune system. NHS sinusitis guidance

sections.title: When to get help in the US
paragraphs: The CDC advises seeing a healthcare provider for severe symptoms, symptoms that get worse after improving, symptoms that last more than ten days without improvement, or a fever that persists beyond a few days. It also lists repeated sinus infections as a reason to seek advice. CDC when to seek medical care
Those time points serve different healthcare pathways. If you are concerned or feel very unwell, seek help based on how you feel and your local guidance.

sections.title: What to bring if the pattern keeps returning
paragraphs: Bring a date range, what changed, and whether you remember days when the symptoms went away completely. If some dates are guesses, mark them as approximate. See recurrent versus chronic sinusitis for examples of how to show gaps between bouts.
AirBloom is being built to put flare notes and usual-day check-ins in a dated history. That could make it easier to recall when you began to feel better or when a new change showed up.

sections.title: When symptoms return after a cold: preserve the sequence
paragraphs: Record when the cold-like illness began, whether symptoms improved and what changed afterward. Improving, persistent and initially improving then worsening courses are different descriptions. The sequence helps explain the history but does not determine a diagnosis or the treatment needed.

sections.title: Three courses that should not be flattened into one
paragraphs: “I have been ill for two weeks” can describe different experiences. Keep the sequence in plain language and use approximate dates when exact ones are not remembered. The NHS and HSE provide general sinusitis information and care guidance; the diary does not replace that advice.

rows: Symptoms became less noticeable over successive recorded checks
The exact cause or date they will end
Symptoms remained noticeable at the checks completed
An initial improvement was followed by a recorded change
A diagnosis or the need for a particular medicine

sections.title: Keep clear intervals and uncertainty visible
paragraphs: Mark whether there was a clear interval, a return to your usual symptoms or an unknown period. “Usual” may still include nasal symptoms. Do not count a weekend with no entries as a symptom-free gap. Add any professional advice already received and the date of that contact.

The recurring-versus-persistent timeline serves the separate question about patterns between bouts. This section preserves the course after one cold-like illness, so readers do not have to describe every episode as a new infection.

sections.title: Use the care route for your location
paragraphs: For the UK, use the current NHS sinusitis page and appropriate local service. In Ireland, use the HSE guidance and its stated care routes. Elsewhere, follow local official advice. Seek advice for a concerning change rather than waiting to complete the chart.

Any jurisdiction-specific duration or escalation wording in this page needs clinical review. The sequence worksheet does not advise antibiotics, change an existing treatment or establish that symptoms are safe to watch at home.

sources.title: AAO-HNS: Clinical Practice Guideline, Adult Sinusitis Update (2025)

title: How long sinusitis can last and when to ask for advice
answer: Acute sinusitis often improves over about two to three weeks. The NHS says it usually clears within four weeks. Look at how the symptoms are changing as well as how long you’ve had them. Symptoms that worsen after improving or are severe deserve attention sooner. Recurring episodes and symptoms that never fully clear are separate patterns to describe.

description: Compare three sinus symptom timelines and find UK and US guidance on when to ask for medical advice.

paragraphs: Copy the name or model number from the packaging or device. Save the leaflet or link with the date you checked it. If the written directions seem to refer to a different model, ask the manufacturer or pharmacist to confirm which set applies.

sections.title: Check that each part is dry before storage
paragraphs: Follow the sequence in the manufacturer’s instructions. The FDA describes allowing a device to air-dry or drying the inside with a clean paper towel. The NeilMed directions for its named bottle and pot give product-specific details. Use them only if you have the matching device.

Before you put the parts away, check the cap and tube as well as the bottle. If you still see moisture, check the directions for the drying position and leave the parts to finish drying as instructed. If you notice a crack, discolouration or a part that won’t come clean, check the manufacturer’s advice on replacement.

sections.title: What if the instructions are missing
paragraphs: Search for the model number on the manufacturer’s site or ask the supplier for the leaflet. If the current leaflet differs from what came in the box, ask which version applies to your device. A note such as “tube drying directions confirmed by manufacturer on 12 November” keeps the source with the task you need to repeat.

sections.title: Save a one-line device record
paragraphs: This record is handy when two people in the household use different devices or when you replace the bottle. If you’re considering a dishwasher, microwave or disinfectant, check whether the manufacturer specifically permits it for that model and its parts.

When preparing the rinse solution, use water suitable for nasal rinsing. The CDC safe-water guidance explains which water to use. Keep the solution instructions and the equipment care instructions together so you can find both.

If you also want a record of when you rinsed, AirBloom is being built to keep routine entries together. Put any device change beside the date you made it. The nasal routine log gives you a place to record the device and what you noticed later.

answer: After you use a sinus rinse bottle, follow the cleaning, drying and storage directions for its exact model. The FDA advises washing nasal irrigation devices and letting them dry between uses. For a squeeze bottle with a cap and tube, check the drying instructions for each part before putting the bottle away.

sections.title: Read the label before comparing products
paragraphs: A box may use words such as “spray”, “wash”, “mist” or “rinse”. Start with what the product actually contains and how it’s delivered. If the ingredients include a decongestant or corticosteroid, follow that medicine’s label or your clinician’s directions. A spray bottle can hold saline or a medicine. The nozzle alone does not tell you which it is. NHS decongestants · NHS fluticasone guidance

For example, one shelf might have a pre-filled saline mist and a squeeze-bottle kit with dry packets. The mist label tells you how to use the nozzle. The kit instructions tell you how to prepare a larger volume and clean the bottle afterwards. If a clinician gave you a routine that uses both a rinse and a medicine, ask which product belongs at each step and follow their directions.

sections.title: Check the water and handling for the device you have
paragraphs: If you need to prepare rinse solution, use distilled or sterile water, or water that has been boiled and cooled as directed. Use the CDC rinse safety guidance for safe water and the product leaflet for preparation. A ready-to-use product has its own label and handling instructions.

For reusable equipment, see how to check the drying directions for a sinus rinse bottle. Different devices may have different parts and cleaning requirements. Ask a pharmacist or clinician if you’re unsure which format applies to your situation or you have instructions from a recent procedure.

sections.title: Record the format you actually used
paragraphs: Write the name and “mist”, “bottle rinse” or “pot rinse” beside the time. If you used a medicated spray too, give it its own line. Later, “bottle rinse at 19:30, felt clearer at 20:10” gives you more to work with than “saline helped”.
AirBloom is being built to keep separate entries for sprays and rinses, with an optional note about how you felt later. You can use the same approach on paper with the nasal routine log.

title: Saline nasal mist versus rinse and how to tell them apart
answer: A saline nasal mist delivers a small spray into the nose. A saline rinse uses a larger flow of saltwater from a device such as a squeeze bottle or neti pot. The label tells you whether a product is ready to use, which water it needs if you have to mix it, and how to care for the parts.

sections.title: UK label example
paragraphs: Look for the active ingredient and the latest patient leaflet. The UK MHRA updated its advice in 2026 for nasal sprays and drops containing xylometazoline or oxymetazoline, limiting recommended use to five consecutive days. This applies to those ingredients. If an older pack or leaflet differs, check with a pharmacist. Overuse can make nasal congestion worse. MHRA safety update

sections.title: US label example
paragraphs: Look for the active ingredient and warnings in the Drug Facts panel on an over-the-counter product. For example, the US Afrin Original label identifies oxymetazoline as a decongestant and limits use of that product to three days. Copy the warning from your exact label. DailyMed label for US Afrin Original

sections.title: Keep track of what you used
paragraphs: A short record of the name, use dates and what you noticed can help a pharmacist answer a specific question. If you have two sprays, write the full name on separate rows so the instructions stay attached to the correct product. If you’re unsure how long you’ve used one, give your best estimate and mark it as approximate.
AirBloom is being built to keep the products and times you log in one place. Use the label or your care plan for instructions, and use the nasal routine log for what you actually used and noticed.

title: Decongestant and steroid nasal sprays and how to read the label
answer: A decongestant nasal spray can provide short-term relief from blockage. A steroid nasal spray is a corticosteroid medicine used to reduce inflammation in the nose. Check the active ingredient and the instructions for your specific product. Similar packaging can contain medicines with different directions.

sections.title: Track the transition in both directions
paragraphs: If you only noticed once you were halfway to the station, write “noticed about five minutes into the walk”. If you don’t remember the exact time it settled, write “clear by the time I reached my desk”. The record still shows the order.

sections.title: Compare two trips you already made
paragraphs: Tuesday fits the pattern that made the writer curious. Friday gives a counterexample. On Sunday the symptom was there before they stepped outside. You can keep all three without assigning a cause to each one.

A change in humidity or another exposure can happen around the same time. The NHS also lists smoke, perfume and exercise among possible non-allergic rhinitis triggers. If something obvious changed, record it. There is no need to create a test or deliberately repeat a situation that made you uncomfortable. NHS non-allergic rhinitis

sections.title: If it happens after coming back indoors
paragraphs: Write the first place you noticed the change. “Clear outside, started running once I got into the station” captures an indoor onset. Record any obvious difference such as a warm platform or strong smell. If it continued while you were at home later, add that as a separate observation rather than extending the first time estimate.

sections.title: Bring examples if it keeps happening
paragraphs: If a runny or blocked nose keeps returning, affects daily life or you’re unsure what is behind it, speak to a pharmacist or GP. Mention if symptoms also happen when the temperature stays about the same. For a room-specific pattern, use the indoor conditions diary. If the main symptom is facial pressure on days the weather changes, see the weather and facial pressure guide. NHS non-allergic rhinitis
AirBloom is being built to show symptom entries alongside available local weather. A quick note about the moment you stepped outside or got back indoors adds the part a weather reading can’t capture.

title: Why your nose runs when you go from warm to cold air
answer: A runny nose can start when you step from a warm room into cold air. Temperature or humidity changes can bring on nasal symptoms, including in people with non-allergic rhinitis. Note whether it starts as you go outside, happens on the way back in, or continues long after the temperature change.

sections.title: Copy a room-by-room observation sheet
paragraphs: Place a portable meter where you normally spend time, following its instructions. If you move it, record where. A reading from the hallway may tell you little about the room where you woke up congested. If you don’t have a meter, write what you noticed, such as “radiator on”, “condensation on window” or “strong cleaning smell”. You can still keep a useful record.

tables.caption: Copy a room-by-room observation sheet
rows: Heat, window, condensation, fragrance or other detail

sections.title: Keep three kinds of observation separate
paragraphs: Dry feeling. Write whether your nose, throat or mouth felt dry and when you first noticed it. Add whether the room felt warm or the heating was on if you know. Dry air can cause discomfort, but the sensation alone doesn’t measure the room. US EPA humidifier and indoor-air guidance

Damp signs. Note visible condensation, damp patches or a musty smell and where they occur. If you rent in the UK, the government guidance on damp and mould explains why it matters and how housing providers should respond.

Irritants. Note smoke, perfume, paint or a cleaning product if it was noticeable. Temperature changes and irritants can contribute to nasal symptoms in some people. Keep these observations beside the humidity reading so you can see what else changed. NHS non-allergic rhinitis

If you compare two rooms, choose times when you actually spent time in each. Note if a window was open or a device was running, along with the position of the meter. The printable room observation sheet keeps those details beside the reading.

sections.title: What two similar readings can show
paragraphs: The first two readings are close, yet the symptom notes differ. The third describes a damp sign but gives no humidity number. Keep all three. The figures illustrate how to record a comparison and are independent of any individual humidity recommendation.

If you already use a humidifier, follow its care instructions. The EPA explains how poorly maintained units and excess moisture can affect indoor air. If your concern is when blockage starts after lying down, use the bedtime observation card alongside the room notes. US EPA use and care of home humidifiers

AirBloom is being built to keep symptom check-ins in a dated history alongside available outdoor conditions. Record room measurements separately so you can tell which readings came from inside. Bring a couple of examples to a pharmacist or clinician if the pattern persists or affects sleep. NHS non-allergic rhinitis

sections.title: Indoor irritants and nasal symptoms: add an exposure row
paragraphs: Record what you noticed in the room and when, then record symptoms separately. A scent, cleaning product or smoke observation is not a measured exposure, and one coinciding symptom does not prove a trigger. Include a comparable period with no symptoms when available.

sections.title: Separate the observation from the explanation
paragraphs: The NHS non-allergic rhinitis page discusses irritants and environmental changes as possible contexts for nasal symptoms. That does not show that a particular room or product caused an individual episode. Describe the noticed scent, smoke or activity without converting it into an exposure measurement.

Keep humidity in its own field and name the measuring device if you have one. An outdoor weather-app reading is not an indoor room measurement. Use unknown where you did not measure it; do not infer a dry or damp room from how the nose felt.

sections.title: Use official guidance for the environment itself
paragraphs: For general indoor-air information, use the EPA and relevant local public-health or housing sources. GOV.UK’s indoor-airborne-allergen guidance describes another part of indoor context. Allergens, noticed irritants and measured humidity are distinct entries, not interchangeable diagnoses.

Do not deliberately expose yourself to something to test the diary, and do not use this worksheet to decide that an environment is safe. Follow relevant official warnings and seek appropriate advice for concerning symptoms. The log organizes observations for a discussion.

answer: If your nose feels dry or blocked in a particular room, record where you were, how the room felt and when the symptoms began. If you have a hygrometer, add its indoor relative humidity reading. Keep outdoor weather in a separate field. A weather app cannot tell you the humidity beside your bed.

sections.title: Record the flight in stages
paragraphs: If you only remember that it started before the wheels touched down, write “during descent, time uncertain”. If the flight was bumpy, note that only if it helps place the event. The stage and what you felt are the details you want.

sections.title: Keep facial pain and ear symptoms on separate lines
paragraphs: A fictional example might read: “My nose was partly blocked before boarding. During descent I felt sharp pressure above my right eyebrow, roughly 20 minutes before landing. My left ear felt full closer to touchdown. The eyebrow pain eased by the time I got home, while the ear still felt full.” This is more useful than “the pressure was bad on the plane” because it preserves two locations and two timelines.

If you have a second example, note whether it was the same side or stage. If a previous flight felt normal, keep that detail, too. It’s fine to say you’re unsure whether you were congested before a particular flight.

The printable flight observation card has separate columns for facial and ear symptoms. If the pain changed position, write where it began and where it was strongest. A rough duration such as “better by baggage claim” gives you a usable time reference.

sections.title: Questions to ask before flying again
paragraphs: If severe pain occurred, symptoms persist after landing or the pattern repeats, seek medical advice. For a future trip, ask your clinician whether you need an assessment and what details they want to know about your symptoms or upcoming travel. If an airline needs medical information, check its process and the UK Civil Aviation Authority passenger guidance. For ear symptoms, the CDC Yellow Book discusses cabin pressure and travel-related barotrauma.

AirBloom is being built to keep dated symptoms and routine notes in one history. You could use it to find the before-flight check-in and add what happened after landing. The facial pressure note card gives you a shorter version to bring to an appointment.

sections.title: One sentence to put at the top of your notes
paragraphs: Try “the pain began during descent, was strongest above my right brow, and was still present for about an hour after landing”. Give ear or hearing symptoms their own sentence if they occurred. If you also experience facial pressure during ordinary weather changes, record that as a separate pattern. Weather and facial pressure guide

title: Sinus pain during landing and what to tell your clinician
answer: If you feel facial pain during landing, write down when it started in relation to descent, where you felt it and what happened after landing. Pressure changes during flying can affect the sinuses or ears. Separate a cheek or forehead pain from ear fullness or changes in hearing, even if both happen on the same flight.

paragraphs: This sequence is an example. The exact scope, whether a spray is used and how the visit runs depend on the clinic and the reason for the examination. Tell them about relevant medicines or allergies and follow any preparation instructions they gave you. ENT UK flexible nasal endoscopy · Johns Hopkins Medicine

sections.title: What it might feel like
paragraphs: Some people notice pressure or mild discomfort during the examination. Before it starts, you can ask the clinician to talk you through the steps, tell you if it will involve one or both sides and agree how you can signal if you need a pause. If you’re anxious about the scope or previously found a nasal procedure uncomfortable, say so when you arrive. Cleveland Clinic nasal endoscopy guide · ENT UK flexible nasal endoscopy

A first ENT appointment may also include a conversation and a simpler examination. If the clinician suggests an endoscopy, ask what question it would help answer. If they plan it for another date, ask what to bring and which instructions apply. The first ENT visit guide covers the appointment as a whole.

sections.title: Bring one example of the symptom you want checked
paragraphs: You could say “the left side has felt more blocked on most mornings for two months and smell changed about three weeks ago”. Bring a date range rather than a long list of details. If a flare passed while you were waiting for the appointment, mention what improved and what remained. That gives the clinician context for what you noticed outside the examination room.

AirBloom is being built to keep dated symptom and routine entries together. If you have a long history, you could use it to find the one or two examples that best explain why you booked, then copy them into a one-page summary.

sections.title: Ask how the result will be used
paragraphs: The clinician may use what they see alongside your symptom history to decide what to check next. Ask whether they can explain the findings at the visit and whether they want you to keep a record before follow-up. If you hear an unfamiliar term, ask what it means in your case and note it in the wording they use. Johns Hopkins Medicine

sections.title: Confirm what happens afterwards
paragraphs: Before you leave, ask whether the clinic gives any aftercare instructions, when you can expect results, and who to call if you have concerns. If a spray was used, ask whether it changes what you should do immediately afterwards. Follow the instructions for your own visit and contact the clinic if you’re unsure. ENT UK patient guidance

title: What to expect at a first nasal endoscopy for sinus symptoms
answer: During nasal endoscopy, a clinician uses a thin, lighted scope to look farther inside your nose. For sinus symptoms, a clinician may offer it to look for findings such as swelling, drainage or polyps. Ask your clinic what type of scope it uses, what it wants to check and what you should expect afterwards.

description: See what may happen before, during and after a first nasal scope, and what to ask about comfort, findings and follow-up.

title: Fatigue alongside sinus symptoms: what to record
answer: Fatigue and nasal symptoms can occur together, but a diary cannot show that one caused the other. Record energy, sleep, nasal observations and the practical effect on your day separately, then discuss persistent or unexplained tiredness with a clinician.
description: A dated energy, sleep and daily-impact record for discussing tiredness alongside recurring nasal symptoms.

sections.title: Keep tiredness separate from the explanation
paragraphs: Feeling exhausted during a difficult week of nasal symptoms is worth describing. Calling it “sinus fatigue” can make the cause sound settled before it has been assessed. Start with what you experienced: heavy eyes, difficulty concentrating, needing to rest, or a change in what you could do.

The NHS explains that tiredness has a range of possible causes. Research has also examined associations between chronic rhinosinusitis and sleep quality. An association in a study does not show why you feel tired or establish that treating one symptom will resolve another. Your wider history matters.

sections.title: Use four short observations
paragraphs: Choose a check-in you can repeat without adding a burden to an already tiring day. Keep your own energy labels consistent. A personal description such as “needed a rest before usual errands” is clearer than a score whose meaning changes from one entry to the next.

rows: Your own description and approximate time
What you remember about the night
Blockage, smell or pressure in your own words
Activity changed, break needed or no impact noticed

sections.title: Include days that do not fit the pattern
paragraphs: In a fictional record, Alex has nasal blockage on Monday and feels tired after a short night. On Wednesday, the blockage is similar but energy feels usual. On Friday, tiredness is greater although nasal symptoms are less noticeable. Keep all three days. Omitting the exceptions would give an exaggerated impression of a consistent relationship.

Add context you already know, such as an unusually early start or a long workday. You do not need to monitor every possible factor. The aim is a dated description that leaves room for several explanations, not a personal experiment designed to prove a preferred cause.

sections.title: Summarize the effect, not a causal verdict
paragraphs: For a visit, state when the tiredness began, whether it is persistent or intermittent, how it affects your usual activities and what you have noticed about sleep. Bring medication names and relevant existing health information through the clinic’s normal process. Ask which observations would be useful to continue recording.

Use the NHS tiredness and fatigue page for current advice about when to seek help. New, worsening or concerning symptoms should be assessed through your local care route; completing a fortnight of entries is not a prerequisite. This guide has not been clinically reviewed.

AirBloom is in development. Its planned diary could help organize observations for a conversation, but it would not determine the cause of tiredness. The printable symptom diary and one-page visit summary are useful ways to keep the present record simple.

title: What is SNOT-22, and how is it different from a diary?
answer: SNOT-22 is a structured patient-reported questionnaire used in sinonasal care and research. It is different from an informal symptom diary. Use the authorized version and instructions supplied by a clinician or the rights holder; this page does not reproduce its items or calculate a score.
description: Understand the role of SNOT-22, how to ask about it at a visit, and why an everyday diary is a separate record.

sections.title: A structured questionnaire has a defined purpose
paragraphs: An everyday diary records events as they happen. A questionnaire asks a defined set of questions using a specified format. Keeping those jobs distinct helps avoid treating a homemade log as though it were a validated clinical measure.

Washington University provides the official Sino-Nasal Outcome Test licensing information. That is the starting point for an authorized instrument and its terms. A questionnaire found online may not come with the right permissions, version or instructions for the setting in which someone wants to use it. Check the official source before copying it into an app, a form or a handout.

sections.title: Keep the questionnaire and the chronology separate
paragraphs: A diary can preserve details that are easy to forget: when a change began, which day was missed, or how a routine was actually followed. A questionnaire is completed according to its own instructions. One does not automatically replace the other, and the labels on a personal diary should not be converted into a clinical score.

rows: Dates, observations, uncertainty and practical effects
That a personal scale is validated
Responses made using its defined instructions
That a total identifies a diagnosis
The points you want to discuss

sections.title: Questions to ask when your clinic uses it
paragraphs: If a clinic asks you to complete SNOT-22, follow the version and instructions it supplies. If wording is unclear, ask the care team rather than guessing how to reinterpret a question. Tell them if an entry was missed or if assistance was needed. These details help the team understand the record you actually completed.

Useful questions include: What is this questionnaire being used to discuss? When should I complete it? How will you compare it with an earlier response? Which version should I use? Who can explain what the result means in the context of my symptoms and assessment?

A score is one part of a clinical conversation. This page does not provide a diagnostic threshold, treatment recommendation, scoring calculator or interpretation of an individual result. A clinician can explain how the questionnaire fits the particular consultation.

sections.title: Where to find an authorized version
paragraphs: Use the official Washington University site for current information about authorized versions and permissions. If you need another copy, a translation or help completing the form, ask your clinic which version it uses and how to obtain it. Keep the instructions with the questionnaire so you can refer back to them.

AirBloom is in development and the simple diary worksheets are original tracking tools. They should not be presented as SNOT-22, as a substitute for a clinic’s instrument, or as a clinically validated outcome measure. Bring your dated observations and ask the clinic which additional record would be useful. Clinical review of this explainer is pending.

title: Ear fullness with nasal congestion: what to track
answer: Record ear fullness, any hearing change and nasal symptoms separately, including the side and time each began. Their occurring together does not establish the cause. New hearing changes or other concerning symptoms should follow the appropriate clinical care route rather than waiting for a diary.
description: A side-by-side record of ear and nose observations, with timing, hearing changes and questions for a visit.

sections.title: Describe the ear sensation in your own words
paragraphs: “Pressure in my ears” can mean a blocked sensation, fullness, a change in hearing or a sound that feels different. Write what you noticed before adding a possible explanation. Record the right ear, left ear or both; do the same separately for nasal symptoms.

Chelsea and Westminster Hospital provides patient information about Eustachian tube dysfunction, one context in which fullness may be discussed. Reading that page cannot establish that it explains your symptoms. Avoid using “my sinuses caused it” as the only history, because that wording removes information a clinician may need.

sections.title: A side-by-side observation card
paragraphs: Use actual or approximate times. If you noticed nasal blockage first but cannot remember when the ear sensation began, keep that uncertainty visible. Do not fill the gap with an assumed sequence.

rows: Left ear felt full; hearing not compared
Fictional example; not a fitness-to-fly assessment
Cannot identify a cause from timing

sections.title: Do not turn hearing changes into a tracking task
paragraphs: The NHS hearing-loss page includes specific advice about getting medical help, including urgent pathways for sudden hearing loss. Read that advice and use the care route appropriate to your location. A symptom worksheet is not a hearing test, and waiting for several comparable entries can delay an assessment that should happen sooner.

If you contact a service, describe the change, side, approximate onset and any other symptoms in plain language. Follow its instructions. In the UK, NHS 111 can guide urgent non-emergency care when that is the appropriate route; elsewhere use your local service. For an immediate emergency, use the local emergency number.

sections.title: What to bring to a conversation
paragraphs: Summarize whether the sensation is constant or comes and goes, whether hearing seems different, and whether the ear and nasal changes began together or at different times. Mention a flight or another relevant event without assuming it explains the symptom. The flight observation card can hold takeoff, cruise and landing details separately.

Ask what should prompt another contact and which observations are worth continuing. This guide has not been clinically reviewed and does not recommend ear-clearing techniques, medication or an individual decision about flying.

AirBloom is in development. A future combined timeline could help you keep separate observations in one place, while a clinician remains responsible for assessment. Today, the printable visit summary can carry a short ear-and-nose history without turning the diary into a diagnosis.

title: Chronic sinusitis with and without nasal polyps: terminology for your visit
answer: Chronic rhinosinusitis can be described as with or without nasal polyps after clinical assessment. A symptom diary cannot establish whether polyps are present. Record the terms your clinician uses and ask how the findings relate to your own symptoms and next steps.
description: A plain-language terminology and appointment worksheet that avoids diagnosing nasal polyps from a symptom checklist.

sections.title: Use the diagnosis your care team has established
paragraphs: People often hear “sinusitis,” “chronic rhinosinusitis” and “nasal polyps” during the same conversation. They describe related concepts but should not be treated as interchangeable labels. The NHS explains nasal polyps as soft growths inside the nose and describes symptoms and clinical care on its patient page.

Similar symptoms can have different explanations. Nasal blockage or a change in smell does not, by itself, tell you whether polyps are present. Write “not assessed” or “not sure” when that is the situation. A diary is a record of experience, not a way to inspect the nose or assign a subtype.

sections.title: Separate findings from observations
paragraphs: A helpful appointment note has room for what the clinician found and what you have noticed. Keeping separate headings prevents a possible explanation in an old note from becoming an established diagnosis when you summarize it later.

rows: Exact wording from your report or care team
What the clinician says was examined or reviewed
Do not infer a test result
Dated blockage, smell, pressure or daily impact
Instructions and follow-up agreed with the team
Confirm unclear details with the clinic

sections.title: Questions that make the terminology useful
paragraphs: Ask whether the current assessment describes chronic rhinosinusitis, whether polyps were seen, and which findings support the explanation. Ask the clinician to explain unfamiliar words and to distinguish what is known from what is still being assessed. The aim is a shared understanding, not to arrive with a self-assigned subtype.

If smell has changed, describe when that began and whether it changed alongside nasal blockage. The smell-and-blockage chronology preserves this sequence without claiming to identify the cause. A report can also show what remains unknown and how much of the period you actually recorded.

sections.title: Record the plan without turning this page into one
paragraphs: Care depends on an individual assessment, existing history and the instructions of the treating team. This explainer does not compare medicines, advise a procedure or supply a universal treatment pathway. Use the NHS patient information for background and discuss its relevance with your clinician.

If a report uses language you do not recognize, bring the original report through the clinic’s secure process rather than relying only on a paraphrase. Ask when the plan should be reviewed and whom to contact if the situation changes. This draft awaits specialist clinical review.

AirBloom is in development. Its planned diary and editable summaries are intended to organize personal records, not determine whether nasal polyps are present. The current one-page summary can hold both your observations and the terms used by your care team, with uncertainty left visible.

title: Persistent one-sided nasal congestion: getting advice and describing the pattern
answer: If nasal blockage persistently affects one side, seek a clinical assessment rather than using a diary to decide the cause. Record which side, when the pattern began and any accompanying changes. Follow current local guidance for urgent or concerning symptoms.
description: A care-facing history worksheet for nasal symptoms that keep affecting one side, with uncertainty and timing preserved.

sections.title: A pattern to discuss, not a diagnosis to make
paragraphs: “It is always the left side” is different from “I only checked it on three mornings.” Both can be useful descriptions, but they support different accounts of what happened. If symptoms persistently affect one side, arrange professional advice and explain that pattern directly. You do not need a completed diary before making contact.

The NHS sinusitis information includes care guidance and explains when further assessment may be considered. It cannot establish the cause of an individual one-sided symptom. A clinician will decide what history and assessment are relevant. This guide is awaiting ENT review and does not provide a diagnosis or a complete triage checklist.

sections.title: Use current local care guidance
paragraphs: New, severe, rapidly worsening or otherwise concerning symptoms should follow your local urgent-care guidance. Use the NHS sinusitis page for its current UK advice; in another country, use the relevant official service. If you believe there is an immediate emergency, call the local emergency number.

A list on a tracking page cannot exclude every urgent situation. If you are unsure which service to use, contact the appropriate local advice service rather than interpreting a blank box or a mild diary label as reassurance. Tracking should support a conversation without delaying it.

sections.title: Write the pattern as precisely as you can
paragraphs: Keep nasal blockage separate from pressure, discharge, a smell change or a headache. For each observation, record the side independently. If the sensation changes side or is absent at a later check, include that information too. Do not choose only the entries that fit your first impression.

rows: Both sides if not checked separately
A precise date you do not remember
Every day when several were unrecorded
That one symptom caused the rest

sections.title: A short handoff for the clinician
paragraphs: A fictional handoff might read: “For about three weeks, I have usually noticed left-sided blockage at my morning check. I recorded six mornings and missed four, so I cannot say it was present every day. I would like advice about the persistent one-sided pattern and what should prompt another contact.”

Bring relevant previous reports and current product names through the clinic’s normal process. Ask what to track next and which changes need more immediate attention. Do not change medication or delay contacting a service to create a cleaner record.

AirBloom is in development. Its planned timeline may help organize dated observations, but it will not decide what a one-sided symptom means. The printable visit summary can already help you preserve the side, approximate onset, coverage and your questions in a compact note.

title: Sharing a sinus diary: a privacy checklist
answer: Review what the diary contains, choose the specific record you need to share and confirm the recipient and transfer method. Check the actual sharing settings in the service you use, and use your clinic’s preferred route for health records.
description: Review your sinus diary before sharing it. Choose the relevant dates and check the recipient, attachment and access settings.

sections.title: Start with the contents, not the file format
paragraphs: A symptom diary may contain dates, health observations, medication names, locations and personal notes. A spreadsheet is not automatically private because it is stored in a file, and a paper copy can also be seen by people you did not intend. Consider the contents and where the record will go.

For a clinical visit, a one-page summary may be enough for the first conversation. Keep the full diary available if it is requested through the clinic’s normal process. Choose the smallest record that still explains your question clearly, rather than sharing an entire folder by default.

sections.title: Five checks before sending
paragraphs: If the sharing settings are unclear, pause and confirm them with the service or the recipient. Do not paste your diary into an unrelated contact or waitlist form. A privacy-conscious checklist is a practical prompt; it is not a promise that any particular service is suitable for health data.

rows: Have I reviewed every field and attachment?
Am I using the correct person or clinic address?
Does the clinic provide a preferred secure route?
Who can view or edit this link or file?
What happens to the copy after it is received?

sections.title: Paper, files and links need different checks
paragraphs: For paper, consider who can see the copy while it is carried, printed or left at the appointment. For a file, check the destination and attached filename before sending. For a cloud link, review who has access and whether the recipient can download or pass on a copy. Confirm the actual settings in the service you use.

A download can create another copy beyond the original sharing link. Ask the recipient about its handling process if that matters to your decision. Do not assume that removing your local file or switching off a link deletes copies held elsewhere. Keep the explanation tied to the service’s documented behavior.

sections.title: What is known about AirBloom today
paragraphs: AirBloom is in development. The existing public privacy notice covers early-access signup and its stated waitlist handling. It does not establish a complete specification for the future app’s collection, export, deletion, sharing, encryption or retention of health records. Those details need to be documented for the actual product before a product-specific privacy guide can describe them.

Do not submit symptoms, medication lists or a doctor report through the waitlist. Use the published contact or removal route for waitlist matters. The blank resources are offered to use independently; they do not require sharing a completed health record with this website.

Before using a future health app, read the policy and controls available for that released version. Ask what is collected, who receives it, how exports work and what deletion covers. Keep those questions separate from a marketing description or a screenshot of a planned feature.

title: A follow-up record after sinus surgery
answer: Follow the instructions and contact pathway supplied by your surgical team. A generic worksheet can record observations and questions for follow-up, but it cannot set a recovery schedule, judge whether recovery is normal or replace individual postoperative advice.
description: A team-instruction and follow-up worksheet that puts surgical contacts before tracking and avoids a universal recovery timeline.

sections.title: Your team’s instructions come first
paragraphs: Postoperative instructions depend on the procedure and your circumstances. Keep the documents your surgical team supplied and confirm how to contact the service if you are worried. If you believe there is an emergency, use the local emergency number. Do not wait for a scheduled diary check or a routine follow-up to act on the team’s urgent instructions.

Kingston and Richmond NHS publishes a patient leaflet about endoscopic sinus surgery. It is useful background, but a generic leaflet from another service is not a replacement for the instructions issued for your own operation. Ask the treating team to resolve any difference or unclear wording.

sections.title: Keep the contact pathway at the top
paragraphs: Leave an unknown field marked unknown and contact the service to clarify it. Do not fill a gap with a generic internet instruction. This record contains no universal schedule for work, exercise, travel, rinsing or medication.

headers: What to copy from your team
rows: The wording on your own documents
Service, number and opening hours supplied
The pathway your team has given
Keep the original wording and document available

sections.title: Record an observation without classifying recovery
paragraphs: Use the date and time, what you noticed, how it affected you and any contact you made with the team. If you are asked to monitor a particular detail, record the measure or wording they specify. Keep medicine and routine entries consistent with the current instructions you were given.

A fictional follow-up note might say: “On Tuesday afternoon I noticed a change I wanted to ask about. I contacted the number on my discharge instructions and wrote down the advice I was given.” It does not label the observation normal or abnormal, or suggest that another person should receive the same advice.

sections.title: Prepare questions for the actual follow-up
paragraphs: Ask which changes the team wants you to record, what contact route applies before the next visit and which instructions remain in force. Bring the original discharge information and a short dated list of questions. If you have already received advice by phone, mention when and from whom it came without assuming it still answers a changed situation.

This guide has not been reviewed by a surgical clinician. It is a framework for preserving your own instructions and observations, not an aftercare protocol. A recovery diary should never give permission to ignore a symptom or delay contacting the treating service.

AirBloom is in development. Any future follow-up organization feature would need to preserve the surgical team’s individual instructions and remain distinct from clinical assessment. The existing one-page summary can hold questions, dates and contacts without predicting a recovery course.
